title: Quantum Walks On Simplicial Complexes And Harmonic Homology: Application To Topological Data Analysis With Superpolynomial Speedups
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kuo-Chin Chen, And Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2138 (2026).

This work investigates whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes exhibit quantum advantages. We introduce a novel quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, a key object reflecting the topology of the simplicial complex. We construct a unitary encoding projecting onto the kernel of the Laplacian, representing the harmonic cycles in the complex's homology. Our efficient construction of quantum walk unitaries for clique complexes paves the way for exploring higher-order interactions within topological structures. Our construction requires [MATH] gates, where [MATH] is the number of vertices, [MATH] is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian, and [MATH] is the projection error. Our results indicate apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup with quantum walks, without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap of the Laplacian is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available. Crucially, the walk operates on a state space encompassing both positively and negatively oriented simplices, effectively doubling its size compared to unoriented approaches. Through coherent interference of these paired simplices, we are able to successfully encode the combinatorial Laplacian, which would otherwise be impossible. This is our major technical contribution. We also extend the framework by constructing variant quantum walks that enable us to: (1) estimate normalized persistent Betti numbers throughout a deformation process, (2) verify a specific QMA[MATH]-hard problem related to clique complex homology, showcasing potential applications in computational complexity theory, and (3) solve the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem (HDDP), generalizing the classical discrete Dirichlet problem on graphs to simplicial complexes, with an apparent superpolynomial speedup over the best known classical algorithm.

.
tldr: This paper introduces quantum walks on simplicial complexes to achieve superpolynomial speedups for topological data analysis tasks, but the connection to the researcher's core interests in quantum information theory is weak.
motivation: The paper aims to demonstrate quantum advantage in topological data analysis by encoding combinatorial Laplacians via quantum walks on simplicial complexes.
method: The authors construct a quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, using a state space of oriented simplices and coherent interference to project onto harmonic cycles.
result: They achieve apparent superpolynomial speedups for estimating persistent Betti numbers and solving the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem, assuming an inverse-polynomial spectral gap and efficient simplex sampling.
conclusion: The work provides a novel quantum algorithm for topological data analysis, but its relevance to quantum information theory is limited as it focuses on computational topology rather than information-theoretic concepts.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that respect a global symmetry, which is a topic in quantum information theory but not a core focus.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define two topological invariants: anyon permutation symmetry and a generalized GNVW index, and shows equivalence to finite-depth symmetric circuits.
result: Provides a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs for finite Abelian group symmetries, and shows the Kramers-Wannier duality has an irrational index and cannot be extended to a full QCA.
conclusion: The classification reveals nontrivial QCA that mix with translations and are not equivalent to finite-depth circuits.

title: Edge-based Mean-field Approximation Of Dynamics On Networks Via Approximate Lumping Of Markov Chains
authors: G\'abor Tim\'ar, Jonathan A. Ward, P\'eter L. Simon
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mean-field approximations for dynamical processes on networks are widely used, but existing derivations often rely either on moment closures or on idealised assumptions about network structure, leaving the nature of the underlying averaging unclear. Here we present a mathematically principled framework for deriving edge-based mean-field approximations for a broad class of Markov processes on networks using approximate lumping. We consider models in which each vertex is in one of a finite number of vertex states and transitions depend on the number of neighbours in each state. Our approach partitions the full Markov chain state space according to the number of vertices and edges in each possible state, and averages transition rates between partitions. This yields density-dependent population processes that, in the limit of large system size, reduce to a low-dimensional system of ordinary differential equations. We demonstrate the method on single graphs and graph ensembles, such as Erds-R\'enyi random networks, and show that well-known edge-based mean-field approximations arise as special cases of our approach. Our approximate lumping framework clarifies the nature of the averaging underlying mean-field approximations, providing a basis for future work on assessing their accuracy.
tldr: This paper develops a mathematical framework for deriving edge-based mean-field approximations for Markov processes on networks using approximate lumping of Markov chains.
motivation: Existing mean-field approximations for network dynamics often rely on ad hoc moment closures or idealized network assumptions, lacking a clear mathematical foundation for the averaging process.
method: The authors partition the full Markov chain state space by counts of vertices and edges in each state, then average transition rates between partitions to obtain a density-dependent population process that reduces to ODEs in the large-system limit.
result: The framework recovers well-known edge-based mean-field approximations as special cases and is demonstrated on single graphs and Erdős–Rényi random networks.
conclusion: The approximate lumping approach clarifies the nature of averaging in mean-field approximations and provides a basis for assessing their accuracy.

title: Separation Of Homogeneous And Inhomogeneous Broadening Using Two-Dimensional Coherent Spectroscopy
authors: Adam Alfrey, Cole Tait, Joshua R. Hendrickson, Steven T. Cundiff
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Separating the contributions of homogeneous dephasing from inhomogeneous broadening in spectral linewidths is essential for connecting optical spectra to microscopic dissipation and disorder mechanisms. Voigt fits to one-dimensional spectra, such as photoluminescence, yield strongly correlated Gaussian and Lorentzian widths, so that neither width can be determined independently with confidence. We quantitatively show that two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS) reduces this degeneracy by providing orthogonal spectral slices, diagonal and cross-diagonal, with complementary sensitivity to homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening processes. As a demonstration, we measure the exciton resonance in hBN-encapsulated MoSe[MATH] at 8 K. A joint uncertainty-weighted fit maps the full [MATH] landscape to quantify parameter covariance. Compared with linear Voigt analysis, 2DCS yields more compact confidence regions and markedly reduced parameter correlation, enabling reliable separation of the contributions to the excitonic linewidth.
tldr: This paper uses two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy to separate homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening in excitonic linewidths.
motivation: Voigt fits to one-dimensional spectra yield strongly correlated Gaussian and Lorentzian widths, making it difficult to independently determine homogeneous and inhomogeneous contributions.
method: The authors apply two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS) to provide orthogonal spectral slices with complementary sensitivity, and perform a joint uncertainty-weighted fit to map the full parameter landscape.
result: 2DCS yields more compact confidence regions and markedly reduced parameter correlation compared to linear Voigt analysis, enabling reliable separation of contributions to the excitonic linewidth.
conclusion: Two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy is an effective technique for disentangling homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening in optical spectra.

title: Nonlocal Transfer Of Quantized Toroidal Magnetic Flux
authors: Alexey Belyanin Adel Ali
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a nonlocal flux-transfer experiment in which a quantized magnetic-field excitation confined within one toroidal superconducting structure is coherently transferred to a spatially separated toroid without magnetic-field occupation of the intervening region. The transfer arises from quantized Aharonov-Bohm-type vector potential coupling mediated by a superconducting loop threading the toroids, which, however, remains in the ground state, acting only through a global fluxoid constraint. A direct experimental signature would be the observation of correlated, time-resolved flux exchange between remote toroids in a SQUID readout. We analyze an apparent signaling paradox related to this interaction as a probe of the broader question of whether spatiotemporal quantum coherence is fundamentally bounded. The proposed setup can provide an experimental testbed for addressing foundational questions such as the existence of an objective collapse of a wavefunction or the fundamental limits of macroscopic quantum coherence which is relevant to large scale quantum computers.
tldr: Proposes a nonlocal transfer of quantized magnetic flux between remote toroids via Aharonov-Bohm coupling, exploring macroscopic quantum coherence.
motivation: To test fundamental limits of quantum coherence and objective collapse models, relevant to large-scale quantum computers.
method: Theoretical analysis of a setup with two toroidal superconductors threaded by a superconducting loop, using quantized vector potential coupling and global fluxoid constraint.
result: Predicts correlated, time-resolved flux exchange observable via SQUID readout, with no magnetic field in the intervening region.
conclusion: The setup could serve as an experimental testbed for macroscopic quantum coherence and collapse models.

title: Measurement-Access Risk Frontiers For Autonomous Scientific Control
authors: Bo Peng
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapidly scaling autonomous science is limited not only by algorithms, compute or data volume, but by which physical records a platform exposes before action. We formulate physically accessible decision-making (PADM) and a measurement-access risk frontier: the Bayes-optimal target risk minimized over records realizable under cost, bandwidth, latency, disturbance, memory and actuation constraints. The frontier gives a no-free-autonomy limit: automation cannot collapse decision uncertainty by computation alone; an optimal controller cannot remove target components absent from its record, and closing that gap requires expanded access, auditing, tolerated disturbance, slower operation or restricted deployment. In monitored feedback, displacement-only control remains exposed to a hidden switching force, whereas a finite-bandwidth cue recovers part of the missing projection before action. A chemistry-aware candidate-ranking audit with a 1000-target stress panel, Gaussian sensing, hidden-regime decisions and cost-aware/thermodynamic channel selection provide reproducible checks. PADM identifies target-specific audit value and residual oracle gaps before deployment.
tldr: The paper introduces a measurement-access risk frontier for autonomous scientific control, focusing on decision-making under physical constraints.
motivation: Autonomous science is limited by which physical records a platform exposes before action; the paper aims to formalize this limitation.
method: The authors formulate physically accessible decision-making (PADM) and derive a Bayes-optimal target risk minimized over records under cost, bandwidth, latency, disturbance, memory, and actuation constraints.
result: A no-free-autonomy limit is established: computation alone cannot collapse decision uncertainty; an optimal controller cannot remove target components absent from its record.
conclusion: Expanding access, auditing, or tolerating disturbance is necessary to close the gap, with applications in chemistry-aware candidate-ranking audits.

title: Enhanced Phase Estimation With Coherently Boosted Two-mode Squeezed Beams And Its Application To Optical Gyroscopes
authors: Xiao-Qi Xiao, Elisha S. Matekole, Jiankang Zhao, Guihua Zeng, Jonathan P. Dowling, Hwang Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum techniques, developed in recent decades, provide new approaches to achieving high-precision measurements beyond the classical bounds. In this paper, we theoretically demonstrate a metrology method for improving the sensitivity of the interferometric optical gyroscope, robust against the loss, by using coherent-light stimulated two-mode squeezed beams as the light source. The detection protocol is based on a simple intensity measurement, and the quantum noise is far below the shot-noise limit. The enhancement factors for different coherent light fields are analyzed in detail. Additionally, the influence of loss during the propagation in the optical path is studied, and the conditions for achieving sub-shot-noise measurement sensitivity are obtained. We also find that the phase sensitivity of the proposed gyroscope scheme becomes closer to the quantum Cram\'er-Rao bound with increasing of the photon number of the coherent beams.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum-enhanced optical gyroscope using coherently boosted two-mode squeezed light to achieve sub-shot-noise phase sensitivity.
motivation: Improving the sensitivity of optical gyroscopes is important for navigation and rotation sensing; quantum techniques can surpass classical limits.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a metrology scheme using coherent-light stimulated two-mode squeezed beams as the light source with simple intensity measurement.
result: The scheme achieves phase sensitivity below the shot-noise limit and approaches the quantum Cramér-Rao bound with increasing coherent beam photon number, even under loss.
conclusion: The proposed gyroscope design offers a practical quantum-enhanced rotation sensor robust against loss.

title: A Quantum-HPC Hybrid Workflow For Reaction-Center Electronic Dynamics: Application To A Cytochrome P450-Inspired Iron-Complex Model
authors: Shintaro Maekawa, Takao Otsuka, Riku Masui, Juan W. Pedersen, David Mu\~noz Ramo, Yasushi Okuno, Kentaro Yamamoto
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce population-transfer dynamics as a practical validation observable for active-space-derived reduced Hamiltonians in multistate reaction-center chemistry. Using a cytochrome P450-inspired Fe-complex model, we construct a reaction-coordinate-dependent effective Hamiltonian from state-averaged complete active-space self-consistent field (SA-CASSCF) calculations, map it to a quantum-circuit representation suitable for current hardware, and propagate dynamics from the reactant-side ground state. The reduced Hamiltonian reproduces the SA-CASSCF reference with an RMS deviation of 0.030 eV and a maximum absolute deviation of 0.143 eV. As a dynamics-based diagnostic, the product-manifold population p_P(t) identifies a pronounced near-degeneracy region around x = 0.3, where state mixing is strongest. Classical exact time evolution yields a product population of 0.488 at x = 0.3 after 10 fs, compared with 7.26 x 10^-2 at x = 0.2 and 5.90 x 10^-3 at x = 0.0. To enable execution on current trapped-ion hardware, we examine the trade-off between dynamical fidelity and circuit resources through coupling pruning and first-order Trotterization. A coupling cutoff of 0.02 eV reduces the non-zero coupling set from 32 to 7 while preserving the dominant transfer pathways, and M = 30 provides the best practical operating point. Finally, we demonstrate the workflow on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer Reimei. The hardware reproduces the key reaction-coordinate trend identified by the classical model, including the maximum at x = 0.3, where the measured product population is 0.42 on hardware and 0.43 on the matched emulator. This work establishes a dynamics-based framework for assessing active-space-derived reduced Hamiltonians and demonstrates chemically interpretable multistate electronic dynamics on current trapped-ion hardware.
tldr: This paper presents a quantum-HPC hybrid workflow for simulating electronic dynamics in a cytochrome P450-inspired iron-complex model, using a reduced Hamiltonian derived from active-space calculations and executed on trapped-ion hardware.
motivation: To validate active-space-derived reduced Hamiltonians for multistate reaction-center chemistry using population-transfer dynamics as a practical observable.
method: Constructs a reaction-coordinate-dependent effective Hamiltonian from SA-CASSCF calculations, maps it to a quantum circuit, and propagates dynamics using Trotterization and coupling pruning for hardware efficiency.
result: The reduced Hamiltonian matches the reference with RMS deviation 0.030 eV; hardware experiments on Quantinuum's Reimei reproduce the key reaction-coordinate trend, including the maximum product population at x=0.3.
conclusion: The workflow establishes a dynamics-based framework for assessing reduced Hamiltonians and demonstrates chemically interpretable multistate electronic dynamics on current trapped-ion hardware.

title: Fixing Divergence In Carleman Linearization Via Analytical Continuation
authors: Mingshuo Zhu, Hayato Higuchi, Hokuto Iwakiri, Kouki Nakamura, Naohisa Sueishi, Shih-Yen Tseng, Shoichiro Tsutsui
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear differential equations play a crucial role in modeling a wide range of phenomena, yet their solutions remain notoriously difficult to obtain. With the rapid development of quantum computing, quantum algorithms for efficiently solving such equations are actively being explored. One promising approach is based on Carleman linearization, which transforms nonlinear differential equations into linear systems. However, this method suffers from exponential divergence beyond a certain time scale. By reformulating the solutions in terms of eigenvalues and eigenvectors, we identify that this divergence originates from the Laurent expansion outside its neighborhood of convergence. To address this issue, we insert a regularized function to the divergent solution hinted by analytical continuation. We validate this divergence-correction method on both the logistic equation and some other partial differential equations like KPP-Fisher equations and Phase-Field models under periodic conditions. We implement our method for the logistic equation using the Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) quantum algorithm, providing a detailed complexity and error analysis.
tldr: The paper proposes a method to fix divergence in Carleman linearization for solving nonlinear differential equations using analytical continuation, with applications to logistic, KPP-Fisher, and phase-field equations.
motivation: Carleman linearization is a promising quantum algorithm for solving nonlinear differential equations, but it suffers from exponential divergence beyond a certain time scale, limiting its applicability.
method: The authors reformulate the solution in terms of eigenvalues and eigenvectors, identify the divergence as originating from Laurent expansion outside its convergence neighborhood, and insert a regularized function based on analytical continuation to correct the divergence.
result: The divergence-correction method is validated on the logistic equation and other PDEs like KPP-Fisher and phase-field models under periodic conditions, and implemented using the LCU quantum algorithm with detailed complexity and error analysis.
conclusion: The proposed method effectively fixes the divergence issue in Carleman linearization, enabling more reliable quantum algorithms for nonlinear differential equations.

title: High-Precision Method For Characterizing Degree Of Collimation And Beam Quality For Application In Cold Atom Gravimeter System
authors: Nawaz Sarif Mallick, Anju, Aishik Acharya
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Highly collimated laser beam with excellent spatial quality is essential for quantum sensing experiments, where even small residual beam divergence can accumulate over distance and introduce significant systematic errors. In this article, we present the design and detailed characterization of a high precision laser beam collimator developed for a cold-atom Gravimeter system, capable of producing an expanded laser beam with a diameter of 16 mm while achieving microradian level collimation accuracy through a five-degree-of-freedom (5-DOF) adjustment mechanism. The beam quality is evaluated using an ISO11146 compliant beam propagation measurement combined with Gaussian beam analysis to extract key parameters, including the beam waist, divergence angle, Rayleigh length, and beam quality factor [MATH]. The measured divergence angles of 0.006{\deg} (105 micro-radian) along the [MATH] axis and 0.007{\deg} (122 micro-radian) along the [MATH] axis confirm stable and well controlled collimation over long propagation distances. The demonstrated collimation architecture and characterization methodology provide a robust and scalable solution for cold-atom Gravimetry and other precision optical applications that require stable, high quality laser beams maintained over extended distances.
tldr: This paper presents a high-precision laser beam collimator design and characterization for cold-atom gravimetry, focusing on beam quality and divergence measurements.
motivation: Cold-atom gravimeters require highly collimated laser beams to minimize systematic errors over long propagation distances.
method: A five-degree-of-freedom adjustment mechanism is used to collimate a 16 mm diameter beam, and beam quality is evaluated via ISO11146-compliant beam propagation measurements and Gaussian beam analysis.
result: Divergence angles of 105 and 122 microradians along two axes are achieved, confirming stable collimation.
conclusion: The collimation architecture and characterization methodology provide a robust solution for cold-atom gravimetry and other precision optical applications.

title: Exact Flat Bands In A 3d Photonic Crystal
authors: Kin Hung Fung, Yan-Long Chen, C. T. Chan, Qinghua Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic flat bands are hard to engineer because Maxwell's equations are vectorial: transversality obstructs the localized scalar-like bases that generate destructive-interference flat bands in tight-binding models. We show that a three-dimensional metallic network of dipolar cavities joined by waveguide channels--a fully vectorial photonic crystal belonging to space group No. 224--hosts an exact scalar sector, carrying exact flat bands. The twelve-band vector problem contains one self-adaptive radial dipole axis per site whose projection is exactly the scalar four-band Hamiltonian of the same network. A microwave-scale coupled-dipole calculation confirms this scalar-vectorial duality. The result is a symmetry-based design rule for scalar-like flat bands in reciprocal vector media.
tldr: This paper demonstrates exact flat bands in a 3D photonic crystal via a symmetry-based design rule.
motivation: Photonic flat bands are difficult to engineer due to the vectorial nature of Maxwell's equations; the authors aim to find a systematic way to realize them.
method: They design a metallic network of dipolar cavities in space group No. 224, showing that the vectorial problem contains a scalar sector that yields exact flat bands, and confirm with coupled-dipole calculations.
result: The twelve-band vector problem reduces to a scalar four-band Hamiltonian with exact flat bands, validated by microwave-scale simulations.
conclusion: This provides a symmetry-based design rule for scalar-like flat bands in photonic crystals, but the work is primarily about photonic band structure and does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: The Ramsey Community Number As A Renormalization-group Crossing
authors: Alexei Vazquez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Ramsey community number [MATH] is the smallest size at which a network is better described by communities than by none, under a Bayesian detection rule. On the diamond hierarchical lattice we show that [MATH] is an exact renormalization-group crossing: the block-model sufficient statistics obey a linear map with eigenvalues [MATH], the degree-corrected evidence density flows to [MATH] at a community fixed point, and [MATH] is the generation at which the running evidence clears the detection threshold. Degree correction advances detection by two generations. We derive [MATH] in closed form for the whole family. Finally, placing on the lattice the Reichardt--Bornholdt community Hamiltonian -- whose ground state is the partition itself -- we find an exact community-ordered phase: below the ferromagnetic critical temperature the two hubs lock into opposite communities for any resolution [MATH], a staggered order that persists as [MATH]. Allowing each nested sub-community its own label, the optimal partition is a hierarchy of [MATH] communities, so the number of Potts states that best describes the network grows with the network. This hierarchy orders thermally level by level, through a cascade of first-order transitions whose temperatures fall as [MATH], so every stable level persists as [MATH]: the emergent partition is detectable, optimal, and thermodynamically ordered.
tldr: The paper studies community detection in networks using renormalization group on a diamond hierarchical lattice, deriving the Ramsey community number as a crossing point.
motivation: To understand the fundamental size at which network community structure becomes detectable and optimal, using a hierarchical lattice as a tractable model.
method: Applies Bayesian model selection and renormalization group techniques to the diamond hierarchical lattice, analyzing block-model sufficient statistics and evidence densities.
result: The Ramsey community number is an exact renormalization-group crossing; degree correction advances detection by two generations; a community-ordered phase exists with a cascade of first-order transitions.
conclusion: The emergent partition is detectable, optimal, and thermodynamically ordered, with the number of communities growing with network size.

title: Qubo Modeling Of Module Learning With Errors: Stability And Scaling In Post-Quantum Cryptography
authors: Ruturaj Khamitkar, Durga Pritam Suggisetti, Soujanya Chatti, Varsha Sambhaje, Durga Dasari
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography relies on the hardness of the Learning With Errors (LWE) and Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problems. This work introduces a constructive framework for encoding small MLWE instances as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) models suitable for quantum annealing. The formulation jointly represents secret coefficients and explicit error variables within a unified binary optimization structure, enabling their simultaneous recovery from the ground-state solution. Beyond the encoding, we develop a stability analysis of the resulting optimization landscape under additive perturbations. We show that the admissible noise region forms a convex polytope defined by competing candidate secrets, and establish an equivalent characterization in terms of the QUBO energy gap between the optimal and second-best solutions. Numerical experiments on low-dimensional benchmark instances using exact simulation demonstrate correct recovery of both secret and discretized error vectors, and confirm consistency between geometric stability regions and energy-gap behavior. We further quantify the scaling of logical variables and embedding overhead with increasing MLWE dimensions to assess feasibility on quantum annealing architectures. The results establish a systematic connection between MLWE problems and quantum optimization while providing a framework for analyzing robustness properties of QUBO formulations. Although current quantum annealing hardware remains insufficient for cryptographically relevant parameters, the proposed methodology offers a structured basis for studying lattice-based problems in quantum optimization settings without implying a practical threat to standardized post-quantum schemes.
tldr: This paper encodes small MLWE instances as QUBO models for quantum annealing, but does not advance core quantum information theory or thermodynamics.
motivation: To explore whether quantum annealing can solve lattice-based post-quantum cryptography problems by formulating MLWE as a QUBO optimization.
method: Constructs a QUBO model that jointly represents secret coefficients and error variables, analyzes stability via convex polytopes and energy gaps, and tests on low-dimensional instances.
result: Correct recovery of secret and error vectors in small benchmarks; stability regions match energy-gap predictions; scaling analysis shows embedding overhead grows with dimension.
conclusion: The methodology provides a structured basis for studying lattice problems on quantum annealers, but current hardware is insufficient for cryptographically relevant parameters.

title: Contrastive Predictive Coding With Compression For Enhanced Channel State Feedback In Wireless Networks
authors: Ahmed Y. Radwan, Hina Tabassum, Fahad Syed Muhammad, Matthew Baker
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate and timely channel state information (CSI) is essential for next-generation wireless systems, yet existing works treat CSI compression and CSI prediction as separate problems, both in academia and in current 3GPP studies. Consequently, channel aging remains insufficiently addressed within standardized CSI feedback pipelines. In this article, we propose a unified compression-prediction framework that integrates Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) directly into the 3GPP-compliant CSI compression architecture. Instead of predicting high-dimensional CSI matrices, our approach forecasts future latent representations and jointly optimizes reconstruction fidelity and temporal predictive coherence via a combined 1-SGCS and InfoNCE objective. This design enables temporal representation learning without increasing feedback overhead. We present two variants: CPC-before-Compression, which performs autoregressive modeling on encoded features prior to quantization, and CPC-after-Compression, which shifts temporal modeling to the base-station to reduce the complexity of users' devices. Evaluations on 3GPP-compliant datasets from Nokia, Oppo, and CATT show that CPC-before-Compression achieves over 90% reconstruction accuracy with 32x lower decoder GFLOPs than the 3GPP baseline, while CPC-after-Compression preserves an identical encoder footprint and the same 64-bit feedback overhead. By unifying compression and prediction within a standardized pipeline, the proposed framework provides an age-aware, computationally efficient CSI feedback solution. The source code is publicly available at: [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes a unified compression-prediction framework for channel state information feedback in wireless networks using contrastive predictive coding.
motivation: Accurate and timely CSI is essential for next-generation wireless systems, but existing works treat compression and prediction separately, leaving channel aging insufficiently addressed.
method: The framework integrates Contrastive Predictive Coding into a 3GPP-compliant CSI compression architecture, forecasting latent representations and jointly optimizing reconstruction fidelity and temporal predictive coherence.
result: CPC-before-Compression achieves over 90% reconstruction accuracy with 32x lower decoder GFLOPs than the 3GPP baseline, while CPC-after-Compression preserves identical encoder footprint and feedback overhead.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides an age-aware, computationally efficient CSI feedback solution by unifying compression and prediction within a standardized pipeline.

title: Grover-Based Pls: Aud And Beamforming With Artificial Noise In Cd-noma
authors: Soumaya Cherkaoui Deemah H. Tashman
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sixth-Generation (6G) networks will require massive connectivity, ultra-low latency, and robust security, making reliable Active User Detection (AUD) essential for interference control and physical layer protection. This letter proposes a Grover-based physical layer security (PLS) framework for a code-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (CD-NOMA) network, where the base station employs artificial-noise (AN)-assisted beamforming and identifies the active set via Grover's quantum search algorithm. We consider two threat models: passive eavesdroppers formed by detected inactive users, and active eavesdroppers selected as the top f% most frequent transmitters among detected active users. By aligning beams and AN with the Grover-based AUD output, the proposed scheme enlarges the main-wiretap rate gap and significantly improves the average secrecy rate compared with compressive sensing and classical correlation receiver baselines, while approaching maximum-likelihood detection performance with a quadratic reduction in search complexity. The impact of the information/AN power split, the base station transmit power, and the fraction of highly active users treated as eavesdroppers on secrecy is characterized through numerical simulations, and design insights are extracted for 6G PLS under both passive and active eavesdropping.
tldr: A Grover-based physical layer security framework for CD-NOMA networks using artificial-noise-assisted beamforming and active user detection.
motivation: 6G networks require massive connectivity, ultra-low latency, and robust security, necessitating efficient active user detection and physical layer protection.
method: Proposes a Grover's quantum search algorithm for active user detection, combined with artificial-noise-assisted beamforming to enhance secrecy rate against passive and active eavesdroppers.
result: The scheme improves average secrecy rate compared to compressive sensing and classical correlation receivers, approaching maximum-likelihood detection with quadratic complexity reduction.
conclusion: The Grover-based PLS framework is effective for CD-NOMA networks, providing design insights for 6G physical layer security under various eavesdropping models.

title: iSTAR: An Algebraic-collapse Framework For Variational Reduction In Quantum-inspired Continuous Ising Solvers
authors: Dongmei Xiao Bowen Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous Ising solvers embed a discrete optimization problem into a continuous dynamical system and recover the spin configuration by sign readout, but dense interaction evaluation gives an [MATH]-per-step cost. We show that this cost is not intrinsic: during late-stage simulated bifurcation the trajectory collapses onto a lower-dimensional active subspace, and saturated coordinates can be eliminated exactly by a variational frozen-set identity whose couplings fold into an induced field on the unresolved subsystem. We prove large-parameter recovery for the external-field quartic model, the hard-box limit of ballistic confinement, and a robust-margin freezing criterion. The resulting algorithm, iSTAR (Ising Stable-set Tail-Aware Reduction), exploits this collapse by detecting stabilized coordinates and continuing only on the active tail. An online certified implementation on the G-set benchmark preserves the same-seed baseline in all runs and removes on average 64.4% of the dense interaction work.
tldr: This paper presents an algebraic-collapse framework for reducing computational cost in continuous Ising solvers, specifically simulated bifurcation, by detecting and eliminating saturated coordinates.
motivation: Continuous Ising solvers suffer from high per-step cost due to dense interaction evaluation; the paper aims to reduce this cost by exploiting late-stage trajectory collapse.
method: The authors prove that during late-stage simulated bifurcation, the trajectory collapses onto a lower-dimensional subspace, allowing saturated coordinates to be eliminated via a variational frozen-set identity that folds couplings into an induced field. They develop the iSTAR algorithm to detect stabilized coordinates and continue only on the active tail.
result: On the G-set benchmark, iSTAR preserves same-seed baseline in all runs and removes on average 64.4% of the dense interaction work.
conclusion: The proposed method significantly reduces computational cost without sacrificing solution quality, demonstrating that the dense interaction cost is not intrinsic to continuous Ising solvers.

title: Support-Sensitive Bohnenblust-Hille Inequalities And Local Invariants On Hamming Schemes
authors: Andreas Defant, Daniel Galicer, Mart\'in Mansilla, Mieczys{\l}aw Masty{\l}o, Santiago Muro
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate local invariants and geometric phenomena for polynomial spaces of low degree on the [MATH]-ary Hamming scheme [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the cyclic group of order [MATH]. Our main analytic tool is a support-sensitive Bohnenblust--Hille inequality for spherical polynomial spaces, showing that the relevant complexity parameter is the support size of the monomials rather than their total degree. Equivalently, in the corresponding toroidal formulation, this leads to estimates for polynomials whose coordinate degrees are bounded by [MATH], while the growth of the constants is governed by the interaction order of the variables. These inequalities yield applications to the learning theory of spherical low-level functions and also provide the basis for dimension-free comparisons between several classical local invariants, including Sidon constants, unconditional basis constants, and Gordon--Lewis constants. As a consequence, we obtain sharp asymptotic estimates for these invariants in the spherical setting, with analogous comparison and asymptotic results for homogeneous and tetrahedral polynomial spaces. We also study projection constants and the associated reproducing kernels. In the spherical case, suitably normalized Krawtchouk polynomials converge to Hermite polynomials under central-limit scaling, leading to explicit Gaussian limits and sharp asymptotic formulas. By contrast, in the homogeneous and tetrahedral settings a dichotomy appears between the Boolean case and the regime [MATH], where the limiting behaviour is governed by moments of a circular complex Gaussian.
tldr: This paper studies local invariants and Bohnenblust-Hille inequalities for polynomial spaces on Hamming schemes, with applications to learning theory and asymptotic analysis.
motivation: The authors aim to understand geometric and analytic properties of low-degree polynomials on discrete structures, which is a topic in functional analysis and combinatorics.
method: They prove support-sensitive Bohnenblust-Hille inequalities and use them to compare local invariants like Sidon constants and unconditional basis constants, employing Krawtchouk polynomials and Gaussian limits.
result: Sharp asymptotic estimates for local invariants are obtained, and a dichotomy between Boolean and non-Boolean regimes is revealed in homogeneous and tetrahedral settings.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive analysis of polynomial spaces on Hamming schemes, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: From Bit To Block: Capacity Achievement Via Product Coding
authors: Bin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper shows that product coding can convert bit-level reliability into block-level reliability at the same asymptotic rate. The encoding process combines a row code of the target rate with vanishing bit-error probability and a high-rate column code with bounded-distance correction capability. The decoding process first decodes rows, thereby purifying the channel output into a sparse residual error pattern, and then decodes columns to clean the residual errors. We prove that, if the column correction radius exceeds the residual bit-error probability and the column length is large enough for a binomial large-deviation bound to overcome the union bound over columns, then the product code has vanishing block-error probability. Thus a bit-level capacity-achieving family can be converted into a block-level capacity-achieving product-code family. As an application, we construct an RM--BCH product-code family that achieves the capacity of any fixed BMS channel.
tldr: This paper shows that product coding can convert bit-level reliability into block-level reliability, achieving capacity for any fixed BMS channel.
motivation: To bridge the gap between bit-level and block-level error correction, enabling capacity-achieving codes at the block level.
method: The encoding uses a row code with vanishing bit-error probability and a high-rate column code with bounded-distance correction; decoding first corrects rows then columns.
result: If the column correction radius exceeds the residual bit-error probability and the column length is large enough, the product code has vanishing block-error probability.
conclusion: A bit-level capacity-achieving family can be converted into a block-level capacity-achieving product-code family, with an RM-BCH example achieving capacity on any BMS channel.

title: Commutator-Driven Stability Bounds For Periodic Switching
authors: Nikhil Chopra Debanjan Mallik
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Averaged models are widely used to analyze periodically switched linear systems, yet the stability of the averaged flow does not automatically guarantee the stability of the true switched dynamics. The discrepancy arises from noncommutativity among the subsystem generators, so stability certificates benefit from bounds that expose this dependence in a form compatible with Lyapunov contraction metrics. We derive an explicit operator-norm bound for the one-period mismatch between the switched and averaged propagators, in which the leading-order error depends explicitly on the pairwise commutator norms of the scaled mode generators, with a closed-form prefactor depending only on the generator norms. This bound yields a computable threshold for the switching period below which the switched system inherits exponential stability from its averaged model, uniformly certified over admissible duty fractions. The analysis extends to an arbitrary number of switching modes via telescoping induction, and a semidefinite program provides sampled duty-dependent Lyapunov metrics for implementing the certificate.
tldr: This paper derives operator-norm bounds for the mismatch between switched and averaged propagators in periodically switched linear systems, with explicit dependence on commutator norms.
motivation: Averaged models are commonly used to analyze periodically switched systems, but stability of the averaged flow does not guarantee stability of the true switched dynamics due to noncommutativity of subsystem generators.
method: The authors derive an explicit operator-norm bound for the one-period mismatch, with leading-order error depending on pairwise commutator norms and a closed-form prefactor. The analysis extends to multiple modes via telescoping induction, and a semidefinite program provides duty-dependent Lyapunov metrics.
result: A computable threshold for the switching period is obtained, below which the switched system inherits exponential stability from its averaged model, uniformly over admissible duty fractions.
conclusion: The bound provides a practical certificate for stability of periodically switched linear systems based on commutator norms.

title: Spectral-gauge Cuts For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Antonio Sasaki (CMA), Sophie Demassey (CMA), Valentina Sessa
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use symmetric gauge theory to develop a general class of cutting-plane algorithms for semidefinite programming. We formulate a separation problem based on spectral normalizations induced by gauges and derive a closed-form separation oracle. This oracle yields an implementable cut-generation procedure that, by varying the gauge, recovers standard cut families and generates new ones with tunable spectral structure. We embed the oracle within Kelley's method and characterize convergence as a function of the chosen gauge and initial conic relaxation. Numerical experiments on small and large instances of box-constrained quadratic programming and sparse principal component analysis illustrate the versatility and performance of the proposed framework.
tldr: This paper develops cutting-plane algorithms for semidefinite programming using symmetric gauge theory.
motivation: Semidefinite programming is a powerful optimization tool, but solving large-scale instances efficiently remains challenging. The authors aim to improve convergence by leveraging spectral structure.
method: They formulate a separation problem based on spectral normalizations induced by gauges, derive a closed-form separation oracle, and embed it within Kelley's cutting-plane method.
result: The oracle recovers standard cut families and generates new ones with tunable spectral structure. Numerical experiments on box-constrained quadratic programming and sparse PCA demonstrate versatility and performance.
conclusion: The proposed spectral-gauge cuts provide a flexible framework for semidefinite programming, with potential for further applications.

title: Long-time Behaviour Of Dynamical Systems Driven By Bounded Mixing Noises
authors: Sergei Kuksin Peng Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the mixing properties of discrete-time and continuous-time dissipative dynamical systems driven by bounded mixing random forces. The continuous-time systems are reduced to discrete-time random dynamical systems generated by time-one maps, so that the main analysis is carried out in the discrete setting. We introduce a class of mixing random forcings whose conditional distributions with respect to the past satisfy natural regularity, recurrence, and non-degeneracy assumptions, extending the framework previously developed for more restrictive classes of processes in a paper by Kuksin-Shirikyan in GAFA (2025). Under a linearised controllability assumptions on the system, we prove exponential mixing in the total variation metric for finite-dimensional phase spaces. We then establish an infinite-dimensional counterpart yielding exponential mixing in the dual-Lipschitz metric under suitable amendments of restrictions on the system and the random forcing. Our approach is based on lifting the dynamics to an appropriate Markov process on an infinite-dimensional history space and applying a Doeblin coupling argument through the method of Kantorovich functional. As applications, we derive exponential mixing for a broad class of ordinary differential equations driven by bounded and mixing random processes. As an application of our result to PDEs we discuss the randomly perturbed primitive equations of atmospheric dynamics.
tldr: This paper studies exponential mixing of dissipative dynamical systems driven by bounded mixing random noises, with applications to ODEs and PDEs.
motivation: Understanding the long-time behavior of randomly perturbed dynamical systems is important for statistical physics and stochastic dynamics, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors reduce continuous-time systems to discrete-time random dynamical systems, introduce a class of mixing random forcings, and prove exponential mixing using a Doeblin coupling argument via Kantorovich functional on an infinite-dimensional history space.
result: Exponential mixing in total variation metric for finite-dimensional systems and in dual-Lipschitz metric for infinite-dimensional systems under linearized controllability assumptions.

title: Unique Insertion Error Patterns In Levenshtein's Reconstruction Problem

abstract: ArXiv:2607.06181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Levenshtein's sequence reconstruction model plays an essential role in information retrieval of advanced memory systems, such as the DNA-based storage systems. In the model, a word [MATH] is transmitted through [MATH] noisy channels, and the goal is to recover it. Errors occurring in the channels usually involve substitutions, insertions and deletions. Our focus is on insertions. One of the main questions in this context is determining the minimum number of channels [MATH] required to recover the transmitted word [MATH]. The original formulation of the reconstruction problem requires that all the output words from the channels are distinct. However, different insertion errors may lead to the same output words. In this paper, we investigate two reconstruction models where the channels are allowed to produce identical output words even though different insertion errors occur in the channels. These two models, called and , generalize the Levenshtein's model. We denote the minimum number of channels required to recover the transmitted word [MATH] by [MATH] in the multiset model and [MATH] in the non-multiset model, where [MATH] is the exact number of insertions occurring in a channel. We determine [MATH] and [MATH] for all [MATH] and [MATH], and show the somewhat surprising fact that [MATH]. We also provide a full characterization of the words attaining this value and give a general lower bound on [MATH] for [MATH] and a recursive upper bound. For [MATH], we construct codes [MATH] from codes [MATH] such that the number of channels required to determine the transmitted word [MATH] is small. This construction is shown to be optimal for certain parameters.
tldr: This paper studies insertion error patterns in Levenshtein's sequence reconstruction model for DNA-based storage, focusing on the minimum number of channels needed to recover a transmitted word.
motivation: DNA-based storage systems require robust error correction; understanding insertion errors is crucial for reliable information retrieval.
method: The authors analyze two generalized reconstruction models (multiset and non-multiset) and derive exact formulas for the minimum number of channels needed, along with bounds and code constructions.
result: They determine the minimum number of channels for all parameters and show that the multiset and non-multiset models require the same number of channels, which is surprising.
conclusion: The work provides a full characterization of optimal words and efficient code constructions for insertion errors in DNA storage.

title: From Regression To Prior-Aware Inference: Solving The Ilwe Family In Randomness Leakage Attacks Against Ml-dsa
authors: Peiheng Zhang, Yuejun Liu, Wei Cheng, Muye Li, Honglin Shao, Yongbin Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ML-DSA is a representative lattice-based signature scheme standardized by NIST. It relies on signing randomness and rejection sampling to ensure that released signatures are statistically independent of the secret key. Practical implementations, however, may leak partial information about this randomness, and such leakage can transform public signatures into ILWE-type problems, resulting in secret key disclosure risks. Such randomness leakage attack can be formulated as a two-stage key-recovery procedure, in which leaked partial information and public signatures are first transformed into an ILWE-family instance, and then a recovery solver is applied to recover the secret key. Existing work has mainly focused on the first stage by constructing such instances under different leakage models. By contrast, the role of solver in the subsequent instance-solving stage remains under-explored, and existing attacks often rely on ad-hoc model-specific solvers. To address this gap, we propose a unified framework to systematically evaluate different recovery solvers on leakage-derived ILWE-family instances. The framework covers three ILWE instances, including the ordinary ILWE, Fiat-Shamir ILWE (FS-ILWE) and Concealed ILWE (CILWE) under different scenarios. Within our framework, we explore three classes of solvers. Our experiments show that the solver has a significant impact on the secret-key recovery efficiency. In particular, on FS-ILWE, prior-aware discrete-inference reduces the number of informative relations by one to two orders of magnitude compared to the baselines: Compared with OLS, BP constitutes a reduction by a factor of 15.4x-64.9x in noise-free settings, and by a factor of 10.5x-73.9x in noisy settings. Overall, this work provides a systematic evaluation on different solvers in randomness leakage attacks, and presents new benchmarks for future analysis on ML-DSA.
tldr: This paper studies randomness leakage attacks on ML-DSA, a lattice-based signature scheme, focusing on solving ILWE-family instances with various solvers.
motivation: Randomness leakage in ML-DSA implementations can lead to secret key disclosure, but existing attacks rely on ad-hoc solvers; a systematic evaluation of solvers is needed.
method: The authors propose a unified framework covering three ILWE instances (ordinary ILWE, FS-ILWE, CILWE) and evaluate three classes of solvers, including prior-aware discrete inference.
result: Prior-aware discrete inference reduces the number of informative relations by one to two orders of magnitude compared to baselines like OLS and BP.
conclusion: The solver choice significantly impacts key-recovery efficiency, and the work provides benchmarks for future analysis of ML-DSA security.

title: Sample Complexity Bounds For The Jensen-Shannon Divergence
authors: Oren Richter, Adi Ben-Ari, Tom Talpir, Elad Schneidman
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) is a symmetric and bounded measure of the dissimilarity of two probability distributions, which has become a standard tool in statistics, information theory, and machine learning. We complement the understanding of its mathematical properties by presenting an analysis of the amount of data that is needed to distinguish between two distributions, given the value of JSD between them. We find the number of independent and identically distributed samples that suffice for a classifier to determine which of two distributions generated observed data at a desired error rate, for two complementary classifiers: we show that for the log-likelihood-ratio classifier, a sample size that grows as the inverse JSD is sufficient, whereas for a majority-vote classifier assembled from independent single-sample decisions, the sufficient size grows as the squared inverse JSD. These distinct scalings offer operational readings of JSD values and their translation into distinguishability in different contexts.
tldr: The paper derives sample complexity bounds for distinguishing two distributions using the Jensen-Shannon divergence, with different scalings for log-likelihood-ratio and majority-vote classifiers.
motivation: Understanding how much data is needed to distinguish distributions based on JSD is important for statistical inference and machine learning, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors analyze two classifiers: the log-likelihood-ratio classifier and a majority-vote classifier, deriving sufficient sample sizes as functions of the JSD.
result: For the log-likelihood-ratio classifier, sample size scales as inverse JSD; for majority-vote, it scales as squared inverse JSD.
conclusion: The JSD provides operational meaning for sample complexity in distribution distinguishability, but the work is purely classical and not relevant to the user's research interests.

title: Lower Bounds For Pir With Preprocessing From Blackbox Cryptography
authors: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: (shortened for arXiv metadata) We study the limits of single-server private information retrieval (PIR) with preprocessing. Prior work has shown that single-server PIR with sublinear communication requires a linear number of (public-key) server operations per query [DMO00, DH24]. Recent breakthrough works, including [CHK22, ZPZS24, LMW23], circumvent these lower bounds by critically leveraging preprocessing to construct single-server PIR with sublinear query computation. Our work presents computation lower bounds for any single-server PIR with preprocessing that makes blackbox usage of {\em any} cryptography (such as random oracles and virtual blackbox obfuscation). For any client preprocessing scheme where the client stores [MATH] bits about an [MATH]-bit database, we prove the online amortized computation must be [MATH] across [MATH] queries (even if performed in a single batch query). In more detail, we prove that they must have either [MATH] amortized online communication or the server must perform [MATH] cryptographic operations. Our lower bounds are optimal as there exist PIRs with client preprocessing matching exactly one of the above requirements while outperforming the other. Furthermore, our lower bounds also rule out the existence of doubly efficient PIR from blackbox cryptography with sublinear query computation. Our proof framework also supports [MATH] communication lower bounds for three mildly restricted classes of single-server PIR. We also prove lower bounds for symmetric private information retrieval (SPIR) with client preprocessing in the random oracle model and present a matching SPIR construction with client preprocessing using only OWFs during queries.
tldr: This paper proves lower bounds for single-server private information retrieval with preprocessing using blackbox cryptography.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of PIR with preprocessing, especially after recent constructions achieved sublinear query computation.
method: The authors use blackbox separation techniques to prove that any PIR with preprocessing must have either high communication or high server computation.
result: They show optimal lower bounds: either amortized online communication is Ω(n) or server must perform Ω(n) cryptographic operations, and rule out doubly efficient PIR from blackbox cryptography.
conclusion: The lower bounds are tight, as matching constructions exist, and extend to symmetric PIR and restricted PIR classes.
