result: The proposed methods are shown to be well-posed and unconditionally energy stable, with numerical examples demonstrating favorable properties.
conclusion: The unified finite element approach provides a robust and energy-stable framework for simulating evolving fluidic biomembranes.

title: Metagraph-Based Domain-Decomposed Galerkin Reduced-Order Model
authors: Kyohei Shintate, Naoki Morita, Shigeki Kaneko, Nozomi Magome, Naoto Mitsume
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study proposes a metagraph-based domain-decomposed Galerkin reduced-order model (MBDD-G-ROM) for distributed-memory parallel reduced-order analysis of large-scale problems. The method represents domain-decomposed Galerkin reduced-order models over arbitrary domain decompositions using two graph levels: calculation-point graphs for interactions among discretization points and metagraphs for connectivity among local approximation-space subdomains. In the proper orthogonal decomposition (POD)-based implementation, POD computation subdomains are represented as metanodes, while metaedges encode the block-sparsity induced by overlaps between local POD basis supports. Partitioning the metagraph enables the POD computation subdomains to be decoupled from the parallel computation subdomains, allowing distributed-memory parallelization of both offline and online phases, including reduced-system assembly and iterative linear solution, without requiring the two decompositions to coincide. The metagraph also supports static load balancing through metanode weights that approximate computational costs. The method is evaluated for an unsteady diffusion equation and incompressible Navier-Stokes flow around a three-dimensional cylinder. The results show that MBDD-G-ROM preserves reduced-order solution accuracy while achieving high online parallel efficiency. A load-balancing test further demonstrates that cost-based metanode weights can improve computational efficiency.
tldr: This paper proposes a metagraph-based domain-decomposed Galerkin reduced-order model for parallel reduced-order analysis of large-scale problems.
motivation: Large-scale simulations require efficient reduced-order models that can be parallelized on distributed-memory systems, but existing methods often couple the domain decomposition for POD with that for parallel computation, limiting flexibility and scalability.
method: The method uses two graph levels: calculation-point graphs for discretization point interactions and metagraphs for connectivity among local approximation-space subdomains. Metagraph partitioning decouples POD computation subdomains from parallel computation subdomains, enabling distributed-memory parallelization of both offline and online phases.
result: The method preserves reduced-order solution accuracy while achieving high online parallel efficiency, as demonstrated on an unsteady diffusion equation and incompressible Navier-Stokes flow around a 3D cylinder.
conclusion: The metagraph-based approach provides a flexible and efficient framework for parallel reduced-order modeling, with potential for further optimization through cost-based load balancing.

title: Invariant-domain-preserving Limiting With Adaptive Mesh Refinement For Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto Discontinuous Galerkin Spectral Element Methods
authors: Benjamin Bolm, Andr\'es M. Rueda-Ram\'irez, Dmitri Kuzmin, Gregor J. Gassner
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an invariant-domain-preserving (IDP) treatment of nonconforming interfaces for Legendre--Gauss--Lobatto Discontinuous Galerkin Spectral Element Methods (LGL-DGSEM) with adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on Cartesian meshes. The proposed methodology extends recently developed convex limiting and graph-viscosity frameworks for DGSEM to meshes containing hanging nodes. Starting from a conservative mortar formulation, we derive low-order interface fluxes that satisfy the requirements of invariant-domain-preserving discretizations. To avoid the excessive diffusion associated with fully connected mortar couplings, a sparsification strategy based on LGL subcell characteristic functions is introduced, yielding compact interface stencils. The resulting mortar fluxes remain conservative, reduce to the standard conforming formulation on matching interfaces, and naturally fit into graph-viscosity-based low-order schemes used for convex limiting. The proposed construction provides the missing ingredient required to combine high-order DGSEM discretizations, invariant-domain-preserving limiting, and adaptive mesh refinement within a unified framework for nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws. We provide numerical verifications of the properties of the proposed scheme and run challenging simulations that require positivity limiting and shock-capturing.
tldr: This paper presents a numerical method for preserving invariant domains in high-order discontinuous Galerkin simulations with adaptive mesh refinement.
motivation: High-order methods for hyperbolic conservation laws can produce unphysical oscillations; invariant-domain-preserving (IDP) schemes ensure physical bounds but have not been extended to nonconforming interfaces with hanging nodes.
method: The authors extend convex limiting and graph-viscosity frameworks to nonconforming interfaces using a conservative mortar formulation and a sparsification strategy based on LGL subcell characteristic functions.
result: The proposed mortar fluxes are conservative, reduce to standard conforming fluxes on matching interfaces, and integrate naturally with graph-viscosity-based low-order schemes for convex limiting.
conclusion: The work provides the missing ingredient for combining high-order DGSEM, IDP limiting, and AMR for nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws, verified through numerical simulations.

title: Analytic Integration Of Metric-valued Functions In Lipschitz Free Spaces
authors: Roger Arnau, \'alvaro Gonz\'alez Cort\'es, Enrique A. S\'anchez P\'erez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an integration theory for functions taking values in a metric space. Following a Bochner-type construction, we define the concept of free integral as an element of the Lipschitz-free space [MATH]. We establish the main properties of this integral, including duality formulas, and the study of the resulting space of free integrable functions. We also cover when the metric space is a Banach space: in this setting, the free integral has an interpretable decomposition generalising the Bochner integral. We then connect the free integral with the geometry of [MATH] by showing that it always produces convex integrals of molecules. This allows to study extremal properties within the unit ball of [MATH]. Finally, we provide a detailed example to illustrate the framework we develop.
tldr: This paper develops an integration theory for metric-valued functions using Lipschitz free spaces, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to extend Bochner integration to functions taking values in a metric space, providing a framework for integration in Lipschitz free spaces.
method: They define a free integral as an element of the Lipschitz free space, establish duality formulas, and study the space of free integrable functions, including the special case when the metric space is a Banach space.
result: The free integral always produces convex integrals of molecules, enabling the study of extremal properties within the unit ball of the Lipschitz free space.
conclusion: The paper contributes to functional analysis and metric geometry, but is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Efficient Pareto-Front Generation For Electric Machines Using Iga And Second Order Derivatives
authors: Theodor Komann, Michael Wiesheu, Stefan Ulbrich, Sebastian Sch\"ops, Peter Gangl
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multiobjective optimization of electric machines always involves a trade-off caused by various competing objectives such as performance and cost. A suitable design is usually determined by comparing variants from the Pareto front, which has been generated by a large number of simulation runs. This paper addresses the efficient generation of the Pareto front using a continuation method based on a homotopy method that exploits second-order derivative information to achieve superlinear convergence, enabling the fast generation of new Pareto-optimal points within only a few iterations. A key contribution is the derivation of formulas to compute the Hessian with respect to geometry parameters and shape, thus enabling direct modifications of the motor geometry in the context of Isogeometric Analysis. We apply our method to nonlinear 2D magnetostatic simulations of a permanent magnet synchronous motor and demonstrate its effectiveness by optimizing the cost, mean torque and torque ripple of the motor. Compared to a first-order optimization method, this approach reduces the number of iterations and function evaluations needed, making the pareto optimization fast and efficient.
tldr: This paper presents a method for efficient Pareto front generation in electric machine design using isogeometric analysis and second-order derivatives.
motivation: Multiobjective optimization of electric machines involves trade-offs between competing objectives like performance and cost, requiring many simulation runs to generate the Pareto front.
method: A continuation method based on homotopy that exploits second-order derivative information (Hessian) to achieve superlinear convergence, with formulas for Hessian computation in isogeometric analysis.
result: Applied to a permanent magnet synchronous motor, the method reduces iterations and function evaluations compared to first-order optimization.
conclusion: The approach enables fast and efficient generation of Pareto-optimal points for electric machine design.

title: A Study Of Holes: Topological Analysis Reveals Crowd Dynamics Regimes In A Bidirectional Corridor Scenario
authors: Gerta K\"oster Sabrina Desiree Kern
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study harnesses topological analysis in an attempt to reveal structure in the dynamics of a crowd. Topology and in particular persistent homology characterizes relational structures in data through the number of connected components and holes, that is, a loop of pairwise connection with no connections across it. We apply this universal data analysis method to a simulated time series of individual pedestrian positions of a crowd moving through a wide corridor -- either uni- or bidirectional. We consider two pedestrians to be connected, when they are sufficiently close. This approach leads to two matrices containing the persistence signatures for the whole time series, so-called CROCKERs. Despite the high level of data abstraction, the CROCKERs' first two principal components on time-delayed positional data show a clear separation of the different parameter configurations. This holds up to symmetry. Our results support our claim that persistent homology is a useful tool to characterize crowd dynamics without introducing any prior assumptions about the detectable spatio-temporal patterns.
tldr: This paper uses topological data analysis (persistent homology) to characterize crowd dynamics in a bidirectional corridor scenario.
motivation: The authors aim to reveal structure in crowd dynamics without prior assumptions, using topological methods to identify regimes.
method: They apply persistent homology to simulated pedestrian trajectories, constructing CROCKER matrices and performing PCA on time-delayed positional data.
result: The first two principal components of the CROCKERs clearly separate different parameter configurations, demonstrating the utility of persistent homology for crowd dynamics.
conclusion: Persistent homology is a useful tool for characterizing crowd dynamics without introducing prior assumptions about spatio-temporal patterns.

title: Closed-form Fractional Radial Links For Elliptical Mahalanobis Discriminant Analysis
authors: Serhii Zabolotnii
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study binary classification under shared-generator elliptical class-conditional distributions. The log-likelihood ratio is an additive function of the two squared Mahalanobis radii, with radial link [MATH]; QDA is recovered only when this link is affine. We derive the Bayes radial-link family from the within-class radius law and estimate it by a finite fractional-power stochastic-polynomial projection instead of tuning a generic spline. The link is identifiable from the radius law, the plug-in estimator is [MATH]-consistent and asymptotically normal under finite-moment regularity conditions, and the induced classifier is asymptotically Bayes-optimal in an iterated sieve limit. The structural bridge, GAM membership, and identity-link/affine-generator dichotomy are verified in Lean 4 without unproven placeholders. Against the global Mahalanobis-GAM of Ghosh et al. (2025), reimplemented with mgcv REML splines at equal input budget, the derived link is never significantly worse on three UCI benchmarks and is decisively better on breast_cancer ([MATH] global, [MATH] global+local). Across six real financial series under temporal-dependence-robust validation, it is never significantly worse than the fitted GAM and is significantly better on three of five heavy-tailed series plus the light-tailed control. Relative to QDA, it improves the heaviest-tailed series (oil [MATH], S&P 500 [MATH], JPY/USD [MATH]) and ties elsewhere. A closed-form rate simulation corroborates the [MATH] rate and the predicted excess-risk dichotomy between QDA's approximation-limited floor and the derived link's vanishing excess risk. The contribution is no significant loss relative to a tuned global GAM without spline smoothing-parameter selection, plus improved accuracy over QDA where generator curvature matters.
tldr: This paper develops a closed-form fractional radial link for elliptical Mahalanobis discriminant analysis, improving binary classification under elliptical class-conditional distributions.
motivation: The authors aim to derive a Bayes-optimal radial link function for classification under elliptical distributions, overcoming limitations of QDA and generic spline-based methods.
method: They derive the Bayes radial-link family from the within-class radius law and estimate it via a finite fractional-power stochastic-polynomial projection, establishing consistency and asymptotic normality.
result: The proposed classifier is asymptotically Bayes-optimal and outperforms QDA on heavy-tailed financial series while being competitive with a tuned global GAM on UCI benchmarks.
conclusion: The closed-form link offers improved accuracy over QDA when generator curvature matters, with no significant loss relative to a tuned GAM, and is validated on real data.

title: Transcendental Correspondences: When Fuchsian Groups Take Over Basins Of Entire Maps
authors: Kostiantyn Drach, Sabyasachi Mukherjee, Leticia Pardo-Sim\'on
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we initiate a systematic study of [MATH] holomorphic correspondences that naturally arise as conformal combinations (matings) of transcendental entire maps with Fuchsian groups. This construction parallels the recent theory of finite-degree algebraic correspondences associated with rational maps. Our correspondence combines the dynamics of a transcendental entire function outside a distinguished attracting/parabolic basin with the action of a compatible Fuchsian group within it. We show that the resulting correspondence is the composition of a M\"obius involution and the deleted covering correspondence of a meromorphic function having exactly one simple pole. When the transcendental entire function has finitely many singular values, so does this meromorphic function, and its line complex can be described explicitly.
tldr: This paper studies transcendental correspondences arising from matings of entire maps with Fuchsian groups, a topic in complex dynamics.
motivation: To initiate a systematic study of holomorphic correspondences that combine transcendental entire dynamics with Fuchsian group actions.
method: The authors construct conformal combinations (matings) of transcendental entire maps with Fuchsian groups, analyzing the resulting correspondence as a composition of a Möbius involution and a deleted covering correspondence of a meromorphic function.
result: The correspondence is shown to be the composition of a Möbius involution and the deleted covering correspondence of a meromorphic function with exactly one simple pole; when the entire function has finitely many singular values, the meromorphic function also has finitely many singular values and its line complex is described explicitly.
conclusion: This work extends the theory of algebraic correspondences to transcendental settings, providing a framework for studying dynamics of entire maps and Fuchsian groups.

title: Optimal Control Problems Of Stochastic Volterra Integral Equations Under Volatility Ambiguity
authors: Mingshang Hu Bingru Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the optimal control problems for stochastic Volterra integral equations driven by G-Brownian motion under Volatility Ambiguity. With the help of G-stochastic analysis techniques and the weak convergence methods, we obtain the variation of the cost functional and the variational inequality. Under the convexity assumptions, we establish the stochastic maximum principle, which serves as both a necessary and sufficient condition for optimal control.
tldr: This paper studies optimal control problems for stochastic Volterra integral equations driven by G-Brownian motion under volatility ambiguity, establishing a stochastic maximum principle.
motivation: The paper aims to extend optimal control theory to stochastic Volterra integral equations with volatility ambiguity, which is a mathematical finance problem.
method: The authors use G-stochastic analysis techniques and weak convergence methods to derive the variation of the cost functional and variational inequality, then establish the stochastic maximum principle under convexity assumptions.
result: A stochastic maximum principle is obtained that serves as both necessary and sufficient conditions for optimal control.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for optimal control of stochastic Volterra equations under model uncertainty, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Delay Violation Probability Modeling For 5g Systems With Harq Operation
authors: Sangwon Seo, Vishnu N Moothedath, Niloofar Mehrnia, Neda Petreska, Bernhard Kloiber, James Gross
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Meeting the growing demand for quality-of-service (QoS) guarantees in 5G networks requires an accurate characterization of delay performance, commonly captured by the delay violation probability (DVP) at a specified delay target. Although hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ) is a fundamental reliability mechanism in wireless systems and is central to supporting QoS, many existing approaches to DVP prediction for HARQ remain overly simplified. In particular, they omit important delay components and adopt assumptions that do not reflect the operation of HARQ in slot-based systems such as 5G. Consequently, these models can substantially underestimate the DVP, especially under stringent latency requirements, where the contribution of the neglected components becomes critical. To address this gap, we develop a tractable DVP characterization for 5G HARQ that accounts for queueing, transmission, decoding, and feedback delay, as well as the contribution of Control Signaling (CS) transmissions to the overall delay, under practical timing assumptions consistent with 3GPP operation. Moreover, we incorporate parallel packet transmissions that proceed without waiting for earlier packets to succeed, an essential HARQ behavior frequently overlooked in prior work. Using tools from queueing theory and Markov analysis, we then derive upper bounds on the DVP and validate them against ns-3 5G-LENA simulations.
tldr: This paper models delay violation probability for 5G systems with HARQ operation using queueing theory and Markov analysis.
motivation: Existing DVP models for HARQ omit important delay components and underestimate DVP under stringent latency requirements.
method: The authors develop a tractable DVP characterization accounting for queueing, transmission, decoding, feedback, and control signaling delays, and incorporate parallel packet transmissions. They derive upper bounds using queueing theory and Markov analysis, validated via ns-3 5G-LENA simulations.
result: The proposed model provides more accurate DVP bounds compared to simplified models, especially under strict latency targets.
conclusion: Accurate DVP modeling is crucial for QoS guarantees in 5G, and the proposed approach better captures HARQ operation realities.

title: Discrete Imprecise Copulas And Alternating Sign Matrices
authors: Toma\v{z} Ko\v{s}ir, Elisa Perrone, Nik Stopar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study discrete quasi-copulas and discrete imprecise copulas of minimal range, which naturally correspond to alternating sign matrices. We show that this family is invariant under all defect transformations on quasi-copulas and give a constructive proof demonstrating that discrete imprecise copulas of minimal range do not, in general, avoid sure loss. In contrast, we show that discrete imprecise copulas of minimal range that correspond to dense alternating sign matrices are always coherent, and hence avoid sure loss.
tldr: This paper studies discrete imprecise copulas and their connection to alternating sign matrices, focusing on mathematical properties like invariance under defect transformations and coherence conditions.
motivation: To understand the structure of discrete imprecise copulas of minimal range and their relationship to alternating sign matrices, and to determine when such copulas avoid sure loss.
method: The authors define discrete quasi-copulas and imprecise copulas, show their correspondence to alternating sign matrices, and analyze properties such as invariance under defect transformations and coherence using dense alternating sign matrices.
result: Discrete imprecise copulas of minimal range are invariant under all defect transformations, but they do not generally avoid sure loss; however, those corresponding to dense alternating sign matrices are always coherent.
conclusion: The work provides a characterization of a specific family of imprecise copulas, linking them to combinatorial objects, but the topic is far from the user's research interests in quantum information theory.

title: Proof Of Execution: Runtime Verification For Governed Ai Agent Actions
authors: George Kang James Rhodes
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent systems increasingly execute rather than advise. When an AI agent queries regulated data, invokes effectful tools, and mutates persistent state, correctness is not captured by whether a terminal output looks plausible. The operative questions are whether each step was authorized under a contract, whether the recorded history is tamper-evident, and whether the trajectory can be reconstructed deterministically. We formalize this as runtime proof of execution. An execution is a triple [MATH]: a contract [MATH], an Execution Causal Event Stream (ECES) [MATH], and a replay context [MATH]. A well-formedness predicate and five validator-checkable invariants form the PoE validity predicate. Five semantic guarantees describe authorization, path compliance, null effect on deny, history integrity, and replayability. We prove soundness under explicit cryptographic and deployment assumptions: any PPT adversary that produces a PoE-valid execution violating a semantic guarantee yields a signature forgery, a hash collision, or a quantified deployment-failure event. The Prime Execution Model (PEM) separates planning, enforcement, effect, and recordkeeping into distinct authority planes; a lemma reduces trace completeness to Effector-exclusive credentialing. An Execution Attestation Certificate is issued only when PoE = 1. In a single-node TypeScript prototype, PoE adds approximately 2.7 ms on a minimal flow and 4.4% overhead on concurrent batch workloads; a standard eight-event trace compresses to approximately 1.1 KB; injected Gateway-bypass and trace-mutation attacks are rejected. PoE does not replace consensus, TEEs, or zkVMs; it binds authorization, effect, history, and replay into a single runtime-checkable object so that governed execution becomes attestable under contract.
tldr: This paper introduces a runtime verification framework for AI agent actions, focusing on authorization, tamper-evident history, and deterministic replay.
motivation: As AI agents execute actions beyond mere advice, ensuring each step is authorized and recorded becomes critical for governance and accountability.
method: The authors formalize a Proof of Execution (PoE) as a triple (contract, event stream, replay context) with five validator-checkable invariants, and implement a Prime Execution Model separating planning, enforcement, effect, and recordkeeping.
result: A TypeScript prototype shows PoE adds ~2.7 ms overhead per minimal flow and 4.4% on concurrent batches; an eight-event trace compresses to ~1.1 KB; attacks are rejected.
conclusion: PoE provides a runtime-checkable object that binds authorization, effect, history, and replay, making governed execution attestable under contract without replacing consensus or TEEs.

title: Optimism As A Vulnerability: Deceptive Stackelberg Control Of Ucb Bandit Followers
authors: \c{s}uayp Talha Kocabay, Kerem Yal\c{c}{\i}n, Talha R\"uzgar Akku\c{s}
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithms guarantee sublinear regret for agents learning unknown stochastic environments, yet the same principle that makes them statistically efficient (optimism in the face of uncertainty) induces a predictable strategic vulnerability against an omniscient adaptive leader. Classical strong Stackelberg equilibrium (SSE) assumes that the follower immediately best-responds to the leader's committed mixed action; it therefore supplies no mechanism-design prescription for a leader facing a boundedly rational follower who constructs and acts on empirical reward histories. We formalize this conflict in a finite-horizon repeated Stackelberg game and give exact constructive proofs for a deceptive leader mechanism. In a honeypot phase, the leader pays a finite signaling cost to inflate the UCB index of a designated follower action. In a trap phase, the leader switches to a selfish action distribution while the follower remains locked into the designated action because the manipulated empirical history and exploration bonus dominate competing indices. Under explicit separation and payoff assumptions, the leader's cumulative utility strictly exceeds the classical SSE ceiling, and the manipulation cost is bounded by a regret calculation of order [MATH]. The results identify a formal incompatibility between static equilibrium prescriptions and dynamically learned empirical incentives.
tldr: This paper studies a deceptive leader exploiting the optimism of UCB bandit followers in Stackelberg games, with no connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: The paper addresses a strategic vulnerability in bandit algorithms, but the topic is entirely outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
method: The authors construct a honeypot-trap mechanism where a leader manipulates UCB indices to deceive a boundedly rational follower.
result: The leader's utility exceeds the classical Stackelberg equilibrium ceiling, with bounded manipulation cost.
conclusion: The work highlights a fundamental incompatibility between static equilibrium and dynamic learning, but is irrelevant to the specified research interests.

title: The Oracle's Gambit: A Game-Theoretic Framework For Responsible Ai Release
authors: Christoph R. Landolt, Tobias Lorenz, Marta Kwiatkowska, Mario Fritz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Responsible vulnerability disclosure can secure the defender's head start by controlling when a vulnerability becomes public. However, this status quo is now challenged by increases in capability of AI models, which benefits both defenders and adversaries. When both sides draw their capability from the same AI model, the defender's head start depends on the lab's decision to release the model, and the question becomes not whether to release but how. Existing safety frameworks govern only the deploy-or-withhold threshold and leave the timing of release unmodeled. We cast this decision as a bilevel Stackelberg game in which a lab commits to a window that sets each side's capability over time in a downstream contest between defender and adversary. Defender welfare turns on the capability gap, not the shared level. Handing one model to both sides can trap the defender in a Red Queen's race, whereas a pre-release to the defender alone creates a protective gap, and the lab's optimal window balances this welfare gain against the opportunity cost of delaying release. For dual-use models, the lever is the sequencing of access, not the deployment threshold.
tldr: This paper models the decision of releasing a dual-use AI model as a Stackelberg game between a lab, defender, and adversary, focusing on the timing and sequencing of access.
motivation: Existing safety frameworks only consider deploy-or-withhold thresholds and ignore the timing of release, which is crucial when both defenders and adversaries draw capability from the same AI model.
method: The authors formulate a bilevel Stackelberg game where the lab commits to a release window, and then a downstream contest between defender and adversary determines welfare based on the capability gap.
result: Pre-releasing the model to the defender creates a protective capability gap, while simultaneous release leads to a Red Queen's race; the optimal window balances welfare gain against opportunity cost.
conclusion: For dual-use AI models, the key lever is the sequencing of access rather than the deployment threshold, and the lab's optimal strategy involves a carefully timed pre-release to the defender.

title: ShadowProbe: Language-Extensible Detection Of Hidden Algorithmic Complexity Vulnerabilities
authors: Yuanmin Xie, Xiangfan Wu, Wenhao Wu, Lingyun Ying, Puzhuo Liu, Haipeng Qu, Zhongyuan Chen, Min Zhou, Chengnian Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algorithmic Complexity Vulnerabilities (ACVs) arise when adversarial inputs trigger worst-case execution behavior, causing severe performance degradation or Denial-of-Service conditions. A key but underexplored source is shadow complexity: non-trivial computational costs hidden inside seemingly benign standard library APIs. Because these costs are invisible at call sites, attackers can exploit them to induce unexpected superlinear runtime behavior. Existing ACV detectors often rely on fuzzing, symbolic execution, or hybrid analysis, but they are usually language-specific, require substantial manual effort to construct harnesses, and depend on heavy runtime instrumentation. We present ShadowProbe, a scalable and language-extensible framework for discovering ACVs through lightweight static analysis, automated reconstruction of execution contexts, and Large Language Model (LLM) assisted test generation. ShadowProbe uses a structured multi-stage pipeline: it statically screens for candidate functions guided by shadow-complexity signals, reconstructs minimal executable contexts from project-level symbols, and synthesizes size-controlled inputs to probe worst-case behavior. It then validates candidates using execution-time measurements and robust statistical growth inference, separating true algorithmic blowups from runtime noise such as garbage collection and JIT compilation effects. We evaluate ShadowProbe on the WISE benchmark, where it consistently improves analysis efficiency over existing approaches. We further apply it to large-scale systems including CPython, the JDK, Zig, Rustc, and vLLM, uncovering many previously unknown ACVs, many of which have been confirmed and partially remediated by maintainers. These results show that ShadowProbe can identify hidden algorithmic risks across diverse real-world codebases.
tldr: This paper presents a framework for detecting algorithmic complexity vulnerabilities in software using static analysis and LLM-assisted test generation.
motivation: Algorithmic complexity vulnerabilities (ACVs) are a security threat, but existing detectors are language-specific and require heavy instrumentation.
method: ShadowProbe uses static analysis to identify candidate functions with hidden complexity, reconstructs execution contexts, and synthesizes inputs via LLMs to trigger worst-case behavior, validated by runtime measurements.
result: The framework outperforms existing approaches on the WISE benchmark and uncovers many previously unknown ACVs in large-scale systems like CPython, JDK, and Rustc.
conclusion: ShadowProbe is an effective, language-extensible tool for discovering hidden algorithmic complexity vulnerabilities in diverse codebases.

title: Privilege And Confidentiality In Generative Ai Workflows
authors: Thomas Melham V\'aclav Jane\v{c}ek
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) systems store and process client data in three distinct ways: in the model's parameters through training and memorisation, in the context window during a live session, and in knowledge databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Each mode creates different and often counter-intuitive risks to confidentiality and legal professional privilege, and each calls for specific governance responses. Drawing on the first English and American decisions to address privilege and generative AI, UK and Munir v Secretary of State for the Home Department and United States v Heppner, on the orthodox privilege authorities against which those decisions must be read, and on recent computer science research, we explain the three modes of data storage and processing in terms accessible to practitioners and analyse the legal consequences of each. We then situate the analysis within the regulatory framework governing solicitors in England and Wales and within the ordinary principles of professional negligence, arguing that the standard of effective information governance (and with it the benchmark against which negligence and misconduct will be measured) is changing. Although we write primarily for SRA-regulated practitioners, our data-governance analysis is framed to extend to any jurisdiction in which the protection of privilege or professional secrecy depends on demonstrable confidentiality. The ultimate aim of this article is to help legal services professionals understand salient data leakage risks in GenAI systems and thereby facilitate a more responsible deployment of GenAI on client data and other sensitive material.
tldr: This paper analyzes confidentiality and legal privilege risks in generative AI workflows, focusing on data storage modes and governance for legal professionals.
motivation: Generative AI systems pose novel risks to client confidentiality and legal professional privilege, which are not well understood by practitioners.
method: The authors examine three data storage modes (model parameters, context window, knowledge databases) and analyze legal consequences using recent court decisions and computer science research.
result: The paper identifies specific risks in each mode and argues that the standard of effective information governance is changing, requiring new governance responses.
conclusion: Legal professionals must understand data leakage risks in GenAI to responsibly deploy these systems on sensitive client data.

title: Full-range Binary Classifier Calibration For Stable Model Updates In Production
authors: Konstantin Berlin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detection models running in adversarial environments face a malicious distribution that drifts rapidly while the benign distribution stays comparatively stable, so teams retrain and redeploy constantly to stay ahead of new threats. Retraining tends to change the output prediction scores, which breaks downstream users of the model. For these security-oriented models we need consistent false-positive rate (FPR) across all output values, whereas standard probability-calibration methods target class probability rather than an FPR contract. We introduce a method built on top of existing calibration primitives that targets the whole FPR curve, giving scores a consistent FPR meaning across deployments. On one held-out split, the observed relative FPR error was at most 2.3% from 10% down to 0.1% FPR and 7.2% at 0.01% FPR. The shipped artifact remains under 200 KB in measurements across calibration sets from 1K to 10M benign samples.
tldr: This paper presents a method for calibrating binary classifiers to maintain consistent false-positive rates across model updates, targeting security applications.
motivation: In adversarial environments, model retraining changes prediction scores, breaking downstream users who rely on consistent false-positive rates.
method: The method builds on existing calibration primitives to calibrate the entire false-positive rate curve, ensuring scores have consistent FPR meaning across deployments.
result: On held-out data, the observed relative FPR error was at most 2.3% from 10% down to 0.1% FPR and 7.2% at 0.01% FPR, with a shipped artifact under 200 KB.
conclusion: The approach enables stable model updates for security-oriented models by providing consistent FPR across output values.

title: aiAuthZ: Off-Host, Identity-Bound Authorization For Ai Agents
authors: Sai Varun Kodathala
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents issue tool calls on the basis of text they cannot verify, so any party who controls part of the context can forge the appearance of authority. I evaluate 15 contemporary language models against eight attack scenarios derived from a published corpus of real agent incidents and find that refusal varies from 100% down to 38% across fully evaluated models; the most expensive model refused only half of the attacks despite a twentyfold price spread. I present aiAuthZ, an authorization gateway that moves the safety decision off the agent's host. Before a tool call executes, the gateway verifies caller identity with a per-message HMAC-SHA256 signature bound to a single-use nonce and a timestamp window, and it evaluates a role-based and argument-level policy that the agent can neither read nor modify. Every decision joins a SHA-256 hash-chained audit log, and each accepted message yields an HMAC-authenticated QR receipt that achieves 94% mean verification across eight transmission channels, with zero forgeries accepted in 25 wrong-key trials. With the gateway in place, residual attack success falls to 0% for all 15 models at no more than 0.03 ms of added decision latency. On the AgentDojo banking suite, aiAuthZ blocks all seven attacker-directed tool calls the evaluated agents emit, at the cost of one legitimate first-time payment, while a spotlighting baseline allows two injections to succeed. Across nine in-scope case studies from the same incident corpus, aiAuthZ blocks nine of nine, against four of nine for a policy baseline without identity binding. The gateway does not prevent a model from being deceived; it prevents a deceived model from acting beyond the verified user's authority on every call routed through it. The implementation and all experiments are released at [URL].
tldr: This paper presents aiAuthZ, an authorization gateway for AI agents that uses HMAC-SHA256 signatures and role-based policies to prevent unauthorized tool calls.
motivation: AI agents can be deceived by context manipulation, leading to unauthorized actions. Existing safety measures are insufficient.
method: The gateway verifies caller identity via per-message HMAC-SHA256 signatures with nonce and timestamp, enforces role-based and argument-level policies, and logs decisions in a hash-chained audit trail.
result: The gateway reduces residual attack success to 0% for 15 models with minimal latency, and blocks all attacker-directed tool calls in a banking suite.
conclusion: Off-host authorization effectively prevents deceived models from acting beyond verified user authority, without requiring model changes.

title: Dynamics And Convergences For Markov Coevolutionary Opinion Formation Games In Dynamic Social Networks
authors: Po-An Chen, Chi-Jen Lu, Chuang-Chieh Lin, Jim Shi, Chih-Chieh Hung
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While deterministic variants of the coevolutionary opinion formation games such as the K-Nearest Neighbor (K-NN) game, e.g., in Bhawalkar et al., in a dynamic social network can sometimes be shown to stabilize using potential functions or localized smoothness arguments, introducing stochasticity fundamentally changes the mathematical landscape. In the "K-NN Markov game", network topologies evolve via a time-varying, randomized selection process. Proving whether such a system, as a special case of general-sum Markov games, converges to an equilibrium is a profoundly non-obvious and challenging theoretical question. Multiagent reinforcement learning has been shown to derive Nash (minimax) equilibria in two-player zero-sum Markov games and Markov potential games (along with some price-of-anarchy types of results). In recent work, optimistic dynamics are shown to converge to correlated equilibria in general-sum Markov games while the price-of-anarchy bounds are unknown. We thus analyze playing specific no-regret algorithms in general-sum Markov games for convergence to a stricter set than correlated equilibria. We integrate the convergence analysis techniques from multi-agent reinforcement learning in works of Wei et al. and online learning in a recent work of Anagnostides et al.. Specifically in (general-sum) Markov games, since the regret of the optimistic gradient ascent algorithm would have extra positive terms coming from Q-values, taking care of these terms requires non-trivial extra work setting an appropriate range of our learning rate and deriving the threshold on the number of iterations for convergence or a bounded price of anarchy, significantly different from those in the assumption in a main technical theorem of Anagnostides et al.. We analyze a weaker sense of convergences to approximate Nash equilibria by playing optimistic gradient ascents in general-sum Markov games.
tldr: This paper studies convergence of no-regret algorithms in general-sum Markov games for coevolutionary opinion formation, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to prove convergence to approximate Nash equilibria in stochastic coevolutionary opinion formation games modeled as general-sum Markov games.
method: They analyze optimistic gradient ascent algorithms, extending convergence analysis from multi-agent reinforcement learning and online learning to handle extra terms from Q-values.
result: They derive conditions on learning rates and iteration thresholds for convergence to approximate Nash equilibria or bounded price of anarchy.
conclusion: The paper provides theoretical guarantees for no-regret learning in general-sum Markov games, but the topic is unrelated to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Extending The Ginsburg-Spanier Theorem To Functions And Mixed Arithmetic
authors: J\'er\^ome Leroux Alain Finkel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study sets and functions definable in the three additive theories [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. The Ginsburg--Spanier theorem~ characterizes [MATH]-definable sets as exactly the semi-linear sets. We extend this characterization in two directions. First, we show that [MATH]-definable are exactly the piecewise linear functions (Theorem~), and that [MATH]-definable functions are also exactly the piecewise linear functions (Theorem~). The proofs are direct algebraic arguments using only a stability lemma and the Ginsburg--Spanier theorem. Second, we introduce as the [MATH] analogue of semi-linear sets, and prove that the class of mixed-linear sets and the class of semi-polinear sets coincide (Theorem~). We further show that [MATH]-definable functions are exactly the functions (Theorem~), a new class of functions that are linear in the integer part and in the fractional part of the argument, but with potentially different linear coefficients for each. These algebraic characterizations unify the three theories in a single framework, and the proofs are purely algebraic, without reference to automata or machines.
tldr: This paper extends the Ginsburg-Spanier theorem to functions and mixed arithmetic, characterizing definable sets and functions in additive theories.
motivation: To unify three additive theories by characterizing their definable sets and functions, extending the classical result for semi-linear sets.
method: Uses direct algebraic arguments, a stability lemma, and the Ginsburg-Spanier theorem to prove characterizations of definable functions as piecewise linear and mixed-linear functions.
result: Proves that definable functions in the theories are exactly piecewise linear functions, and introduces mixed-linear sets as the analogue of semi-linear sets, showing they coincide with semi-polinear sets.
conclusion: Provides a unified algebraic framework for the three additive theories without reference to automata or machines.

title: The Balkanization Of Execution-Security Research For Ai Coding Agents: Isolation, Access Control, And Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use Vulnerabilities
authors: Mohammadreza Rashidi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents now read repositories, call tools, and execute shell commands with limited human oversight, and a fast-growing body of work studies whether the execution layer around them is actually safe. That literature is scattered. Papers on sandbox isolation, capability and access control, policy enforcement, time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) races, Model Context Protocol (MCP) threats, identity delegation, execution provenance, network egress control, and static analysis of agent-generated code are published independently and rarely cite one another. We systematize 39 papers published between 2023 and 2026 into 17 categories, each verified directly against its source. The same verification protocol also confirms four disclosed, patched CVEs directly affecting production agent harnesses. Reading across categories surfaces five cross-cutting gaps that no single paper addresses. (1) Isolation architectures and capability models are almost never evaluated against one another on a shared benchmark. (2) Policy-enforcement studies report failure rates from 69% to 98% of real denylists, yet no isolation paper re-evaluates its own defense under that adversarial setting. (3) TOCTOU and MCP threats are analyzed as separate literatures despite both being instances of the same state-validation problem. (4) Every enforcement mechanism assumes an honest policy author, leaving policy-authoring error itself unaddressed. (5) Benign but out-of-scope agent actions occurring at rates up to 17.1% under realistic prompting are addressed by no access-control or capability paper in the corpus. Existing broader surveys of agentic AI security discuss sandboxing only as one item among many defenses, leaving execution security without a dedicated systematization. This paper is written to fill that gap. We conclude with a research agenda directed at the five gaps.
tldr: This paper systematizes execution-security research for AI coding agents, focusing on sandbox isolation, access control, and TOCTOU vulnerabilities.
motivation: The literature on execution security for AI coding agents is scattered across multiple subfields that rarely cite each other, leaving cross-cutting gaps unaddressed.
method: The authors systematize 39 papers published between 2023 and 2026 into 17 categories, verify disclosed CVEs, and identify five cross-cutting gaps.
result: Five gaps are identified: lack of shared benchmarks, isolation not re-evaluated under adversarial settings, TOCTOU and MCP threats not unified, policy-authoring errors ignored, and benign out-of-scope actions unaddressed.
conclusion: The paper provides a dedicated systematization of execution security for AI coding agents and proposes a research agenda to address the identified gaps.

title: Unicode TAG-Block Concealment Of Tool-Metadata Payloads In The Model Context Protocol: An Approval-View Fidelity Gap Across Three Independent Server Implementations
authors: Mohammadreza Rashidi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the dominant way coding agents discover and invoke external tools. A server advertises each tool through a tools/list handshake that returns a name, a natural-language description, and a JSON input schema. The client renders this metadata once, in a one-time approval dialog, and then injects it verbatim into the model's context on every subsequent turn. Nothing in the protocol requires the rendered approval view and the bytes delivered to the model to match. We isolate that gap as a single structural mechanism, concealment encoding, and show with a model-free, protocol-free analysis that Unicode's TAG block (U+E0000 to U+E007F) has no assigned glyph in any mainstream terminal, chat, or IDE renderer, so a payload written in it is absent from what a human reviewer sees while surviving byte-for-byte into the model's tokenizer. We then measure whether this mechanism actually defeats today's client-side defenses, building a proof-of-concept that speaks the real MCP JSON-RPC/stdio protocol against a genuine client and server. Across 5 distinct MCP metadata surfaces we implement 8 concrete techniques with a deterministic, protocol-level harness. All 8/8 techniques deliver an attacker-controlled payload into the model's context, 4/8 evade a representative string-matching sanitizer, and exactly as the mechanism analysis predicts, only the TAG-block encoding (1/8) is invisible in the human approval view while still reaching the model verbatim. MCP forces re-approval for 0/8 techniques even under a time-of-check to time-of-use rug-pull. To test whether these outcomes are a property of the protocol or an artifact of one server codebase, we re-implement the catalogue against 3 independently developed Python MCP server libraries and find total agreement across all 32 cross-library outcome cells. The baseline sanitizer flags 0 of 25 benign descriptions.
tldr: This paper studies a security vulnerability in the Model Context Protocol where Unicode TAG-block characters can hide tool metadata from human reviewers while being passed to the AI model.
motivation: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is widely used by coding agents to invoke external tools, but there is a gap between what human reviewers see in approval dialogs and what the model receives, potentially allowing malicious payloads.
method: The authors analyze the Unicode TAG block (U+E0000–U+E007F) which has no visible glyph in mainstream renderers, implement 8 concealment techniques across 5 MCP metadata surfaces, and test them against a real client and server, as well as three independent server libraries.
result: All 8 techniques successfully deliver attacker-controlled payloads into the model's context; 4 evade a string-matching sanitizer; only the TAG-block encoding is invisible in the approval view; results are consistent across all three server implementations.
conclusion: The MCP protocol has a fundamental security gap that can be exploited via Unicode concealment, and current client-side defenses are insufficient.

title: Contextual Procurement Auctions With Bandit Learning
authors: Yiling Chen, Shi Feng, Sadie Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study repeated contextual procurement auctions in which the platform must learn context-dependent product values from bandit feedback. We give an exactly truthful explore-then-commit mechanism with [MATH] regret. We also give a frozen-payment UCB mechanism with a regret-incentive tradeoff: the near-UCB tuning attains \(\widetilde O()\) welfare regret, while for fixed \(n,g\) its total incentive error is \(\widetilde O(T^{3/4})\); the balanced tuning gives \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3})\) on both scales. Regret is measured as welfare loss relative to the full-information efficient allocation. We prove a matching lower bound for the frozen-payment regret-incentive tradeoff.
tldr: This paper studies repeated contextual procurement auctions with bandit learning, focusing on regret and incentive compatibility.
motivation: The authors aim to design mechanisms for procurement auctions where the platform must learn product values from bandit feedback while ensuring truthfulness.
method: They propose an exactly truthful explore-then-commit mechanism and a frozen-payment UCB mechanism, analyzing regret and incentive tradeoffs.
result: The explore-then-commit mechanism achieves O(T^{2/3}) regret; the frozen-payment UCB mechanism offers a regret-incentive tradeoff with near-UCB tuning achieving O(T^{1/2}) welfare regret and O(T^{3/4}) incentive error, while balanced tuning gives O(T^{2/3}) on both scales.
conclusion: The paper provides theoretical bounds and a matching lower bound for the frozen-payment regret-incentive tradeoff, contributing to auction theory and bandit learning.

title: Withdrawability In Fiat-Shamir With Aborts Constructions
authors: Ramses Fernandez-Valencia
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents an extension of the work performed by Liu, Baek and Susilo on withdrawable signatures to the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm. We introduce an abstract construction, and provide security proofs for this proposal. As an instantiation, we provide a concrete withdrawable signature scheme based on a no-hint, full-t Dilithium-style Fiat-Shamir with aborts construction; adapting to production ML-DSA (with hints) introduces a small epsilon term.
tldr: This paper extends withdrawable signatures to the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm, providing an abstract construction and a concrete scheme based on Dilithium-style signatures.
motivation: The authors aim to extend the concept of withdrawable signatures to the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm, which is used in lattice-based signatures like Dilithium.
method: The paper presents an abstract construction of withdrawable signatures within the Fiat-Shamir with aborts framework and provides security proofs. It also instantiates the scheme using a no-hint, full-t Dilithium-style construction.
result: A concrete withdrawable signature scheme is provided, with an epsilon term introduced when adapting to production ML-DSA with hints.
conclusion: The work extends withdrawable signatures to a new paradigm, but the contribution is primarily cryptographic and not related to quantum information theory or the specified research directions.

title: MSCENet: A Multi-Scale Correlation Enhanced Network For Anomaly Detection
authors: Long Zhao, Shixun Ji, Zhipeng Wang, Bin Cheng, Bin He
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the field of multivariate time series anomaly detection, against the backdrop of increasing data complexity and complex dependencies across multiple temporal scales, traditional methods often struggle to simultaneously capture temporal dynamic features and intricate inter-series correlations. To address this, we propose an innovative framework, MSCENet, which leverages advanced spatio-temporal learning and multi-scale learning techniques to enhance detection accuracy. MSCENet includes a fine-grained temporal convolution module that captures complex temporal dependencies through dilated convolutions, enabling the detection of both short- and long-term patterns. Additionally, the framework models inter-series relationships as a graph structure, using Mixhop graph convolutions to adaptively capture spatial dependencies across varying time scales. To support robust anomaly detection, the multi-scale gated convolution module in MSCENet integrates spatial and temporal attributes through gated mechanisms, facilitating the detection of subtle variations across multiple scales. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets: SMD, PSM, and SWaT. It provides an adaptable and high-performance solution for anomaly detection in complex time series data environments.
tldr: This paper proposes a multi-scale correlation enhanced network for anomaly detection in multivariate time series, which is unrelated to quantum information theory or quantum physics.
motivation: Traditional methods struggle to capture temporal dynamics and inter-series correlations in complex multivariate time series data.
method: MSCENet uses fine-grained temporal convolution with dilated convolutions, Mixhop graph convolutions for spatial dependencies, and multi-scale gated convolution modules to integrate spatial and temporal attributes.
result: Experimental evaluations on SMD, PSM, and SWaT datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness for anomaly detection.
conclusion: MSCENet provides an adaptable and high-performance solution for anomaly detection in complex time series data.

title: Code-Level Cost Function Generation For Spatial Image Steganography Using RAG-Enhanced Large Language Models
authors: Yige Wang, Shiqi Yi, Hanzhou Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing cost functions of adaptive steganography traditionally requires extensive manual tuning, while deep learning methods lack interpretability. Although large language models (LLMs) offer an automated alternative via evolutionary generation, they often violate domain specific mathematical constraints due to a lack of explicit domain knowledge. To address this problem, we propose a novel evolutionary system focused on exploiting Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhanced LLMs for the automatic code-level generation of spatial steganography cost functions. This system incorporates a core Self Evolving RAG (SE-RAG) module, wherein a Code Semantic Signature (CSS) translates procedural code into aligned queries, retrieving explicit guidance from static literature and dynamic experience knowledge bases to steer the LLM generation process. A dedicated feedback mechanism then continuously refines the dynamic knowledge base with successful optimization strategies. Extensive experiments on the BOSSBase and BOWS2 datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves higher steganographic security than existing automatically designed methods, and increases the average code execution rate by 46.3% while reducing the search cost by 26.1%, thereby highlighting the effectiveness, efficiency, and potential of combining LLMs with domain-specific knowledge in the field of automatic steganographic algorithm generation.
tldr: This paper uses RAG-enhanced LLMs to automatically generate cost functions for spatial image steganography, improving security and efficiency.
motivation: Designing cost functions for adaptive steganography is labor-intensive and deep learning methods lack interpretability; LLMs offer automation but often violate domain constraints.
method: A Self Evolving RAG (SE-RAG) module with Code Semantic Signature (CSS) translates code into queries, retrieves guidance from static and dynamic knowledge bases, and refines the dynamic base via feedback.
result: The framework achieves higher steganographic security than existing automated methods, increases code execution rate by 46.3%, and reduces search cost by 26.1%.
conclusion: Combining LLMs with domain-specific knowledge effectively automates steganographic algorithm generation with improved performance.

title: i-EXAM: Instructable And Explainable Attack Connectivity Graph Modeler
authors: Rakesh Podder, Wadia Ganim, Sarath Sreedharan, Indrajit Ray, Indrakshi Ray
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: i-EXAM is a planning-powered tool that helps system administrators to create security profiles of complex networks and perform what-if analyses to identify network hardening strategies. It leverages planning compilation that provides soundness and completeness guarantees to identify attack paths, evaluate security metrics, generate diverse hardening strategies, and explain these strategies in natural language using Large Language Models.
tldr: i-EXAM is a planning-powered tool for network security profiling and hardening strategy generation using LLMs.
motivation: System administrators need automated tools to identify attack paths and hardening strategies in complex networks.
method: The tool uses planning compilation with soundness and completeness guarantees to model attack connectivity, evaluate security metrics, and generate diverse hardening strategies, with explanations produced by large language models.
result: The approach provides sound and complete identification of attack paths and generates natural language explanations for hardening strategies.
conclusion: i-EXAM offers a practical tool for network security management, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Teaching Ltl And {\omega}-automata With Spot
authors: Alexandre Duret-Lutz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spot is a mature, open-source C++/Python library and toolset for Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) and [MATH]-automata manipulation. While Spot is routinely used as a research and verification back-end, its rich visualization capabilities and Python interface also make it an attractive platform for the connections between temporal logic formulas and the [MATH]-automata that give them their semantics.
tldr: This paper presents Spot, a library for LTL and ω-automata manipulation, focusing on teaching and visualization.
motivation: To provide an educational tool for understanding the connection between temporal logic formulas and automata.
method: Describes the features of Spot, including its C++/Python library and visualization capabilities.
result: Spot is a mature tool that can be used for both research and teaching.
conclusion: Spot is an attractive platform for teaching LTL and ω-automata due to its rich visualization and Python interface.

title: Reproducible Validation Of Voucher-Based L2 Interoperability: Diagnosing An Erc-4337 Compatibility Issue In An Eil Sdk Implementation
authors: Cheng-En Lee, Yu-Chien Huang, Yun-Cheng Tsai
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ethereum Layer-2 (L2) ecosystems improve scalability but also fragment users, liquidity, gas funding, and execution across rollups. Consequently, cross-rollup interoperability is not only a bridging problem but also a wallet, execution, and validation problem. Ethereum Interop Layer (EIL) proposes a voucher-based architecture in which users create voucher requests on an origin chain and redeem XLP-signed vouchers on a destination chain. When reproducing the evaluated SDK version in a controlled local environment, we observed a compatibility issue in the path: paymaster-related data can differ after signing, preventing a stable comparison between the user-authorized representation and the representation later inspected by the local validation flow. This paper presents a reproducible two-L2 validation framework and a controlled compatibility mitigation for that issue. We build a deterministic local testbed over Arbitrum- and Optimism-style development chains, deploy the core paymaster and bridge-related components, implement mock bundlers and event-driven XLP providers, and introduce a sanitized paymaster-data handling path together with a compatible multichain account wrapper. Using this framework, we execute the core voucher lifecycle from request creation to destination-chain voucher redemption and asset release. The contribution is an empirical diagnosis of an implementation-level compatibility barrier, a bounded mitigation that restores controlled end-to-end execution, and an inspectable validation artifact for studying voucher-based interoperability. The work does not claim a new interoperability protocol, universal wallet compatibility, or production readiness; it identifies the remaining gaps toward standard-account validation, one-signature multichain authorization, and full dispute-settlement support.
tldr: This paper diagnoses and mitigates a paymaster-data compatibility issue in an Ethereum Layer-2 interoperability SDK, focusing on voucher-based cross-rollup validation.
motivation: Ethereum L2 ecosystems suffer from fragmentation, and voucher-based interoperability requires reproducible validation to ensure compatibility across rollups.
method: The authors build a deterministic local testbed over Arbitrum- and Optimism-style chains, deploy core components, implement mock bundlers and XLP providers, and introduce a sanitized paymaster-data handling path with a compatible multichain account wrapper.
result: They identify a compatibility issue where paymaster data can differ after signing, and implement a bounded mitigation that restores controlled end-to-end execution.
conclusion: The work provides an empirical diagnosis and mitigation for an implementation-level barrier, but does not claim a new protocol or production readiness.

title: A Lower Bound For Read-Once Parity Branching Programs
authors: Ben Lee Volk
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove an [MATH] lower bound for read-once parity branching programs computing an explicit boolean function on [MATH] variables. The previous best lower bound was [MATH]. Our lower bound is proved by reducing the problem to a lower bound in algebraic circuit complexity.
tldr: This paper proves a lower bound for read-once parity branching programs, a topic in computational complexity theory.
motivation: Understanding the power of restricted branching programs is a fundamental question in complexity theory.
method: The lower bound is obtained by reducing the problem to a lower bound in algebraic circuit complexity.
result: An explicit boolean function on n variables requires read-once parity branching programs of size at least n^{3/2} / polylog(n).
conclusion: The result improves the previous best lower bound and demonstrates a connection between branching program complexity and algebraic circuit complexity.

title: Formalizing Scarf, Brouwer, And Nash In Lean
authors: Kai Li Yuwei Lyu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.05987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formalize in Lean 4 a complete combinatorial route from Scarf's theorem to Brouwer's fixed point theorem and to the existence of mixed Nash equilibria in finite games. The development follows Ivanov's indexed-order formulation of Scarf's theorem, formalizes the room--door incidence structure and parity argument, instantiates the theorem on finite grids of the standard simplex, and carries out the compactness and continuity argument needed to obtain a fixed point. We then extend the result to finite products of simplices by an explicit embedding--projection construction and use this product theorem to prove mixed Nash equilibrium existence via the Nash map. As a secondary by-product, we derive BrouwerBench, a preliminary 80-item Lean-grounded benchmark for probing proof-structure understanding within this single formal development.
tldr: This paper formalizes combinatorial proofs of Scarf's theorem, Brouwer's fixed point theorem, and Nash equilibrium existence in the Lean 4 theorem prover.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a complete formalization of fundamental fixed point theorems and their application to game theory, and to create a benchmark for proof-structure understanding.
method: The formalization follows Ivanov's indexed-order formulation of Scarf's theorem, uses a room-door incidence structure and parity argument, instantiates on finite grids of the simplex, and extends to products via embedding-projection.
result: The formalization successfully proves Brouwer's fixed point theorem and the existence of mixed Nash equilibria in finite games, and produces BrouwerBench, an 80-item benchmark.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of formalizing advanced combinatorial and game-theoretic proofs in Lean, but is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Context-to-Execution Integrity For Llm Agents
authors: Igor Santos-Grueiro
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents read attacker-writable context to solve tasks. Tool execution needs a separate authority check for protected sink fields, sink-interpreted payloads, and the invocation event. Context-to-Execution Integrity (CXI) is an execution-boundary system for this setting. Policies mark protected sink fields, typed releases carry narrow validated values from writable context to specific destinations, opaque data slots keep evidence as data, and a deterministic gate admits a call only after field authority, exact-effect authorization, and invocation authority all bind to the same action manifest. We evaluate CXI on open-weight field-projection runs, AgentDojo live episodes, a code-agent exact-effect benchmark, manifest-bound ledger faults, proposal-pressure controls, and hosted/API compatibility traces. AgentDojo covers 720 live episodes and 1,739 LLM calls; the code-agent benchmark covers 400 repository episodes with exact-effect authorization and lease-bound execution, yielding 231 safe task completions and zero observed field, effect, or invocation escapes. The accounting reports parser outcomes, authorization outcomes, and task-quality outcomes together with the admission-integrity result. Across the evaluated sinks, CXI admits execution only when field, effect, and invocation authority bind to the same action manifest.
tldr: This paper proposes Context-to-Execution Integrity (CXI), a system to ensure that LLM agents execute tool calls only when authorized by a policy, preventing context injection attacks.
motivation: LLM agents read attacker-writable context and execute tools, creating a security risk where context can be manipulated to trigger unauthorized tool calls. Existing systems lack a unified authority check for sink fields, payloads, and invocation events.
method: CXI introduces an execution-boundary system with policies marking protected sink fields, typed releases carrying validated values, opaque data slots for evidence, and a deterministic gate that admits a call only after field authority, exact-effect authorization, and invocation authority all bind to the same action manifest.
result: Evaluated on AgentDojo (720 live episodes, 1,739 LLM calls) and a code-agent benchmark (400 repository episodes), CXI achieved 231 safe task completions with zero observed field, effect, or invocation escapes.
conclusion: CXI effectively prevents context-to-execution integrity violations in LLM agents, providing a robust security mechanism for tool execution.

title: Rean: Reconstruction-aware Ecg Anonymization Based On Privacy--Utility Orthogonality
authors: Taerin Ki, Sunghwan Park, Junyoung Park, Jaewoo Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A shared electrocardiogram (ECG) is itself a biometric fingerprint that can re-identify a patient and reveal personal information. Recent ECG anonymizers transform the signal before sharing to reduce privacy leakage. However, existing methods still face a privacy--utility trade-off, in which preserving privacy often compromises utility while preserving utility reveals personal information. We propose (construction-aware ECG onymizer), a raw ECG signal anonymizer, to address this privacy--utility trade-off. REAN reconstructs the signal using a 1-D U-Net trained with losses from frozen privacy and utility classifiers to reduce privacy leakage while preserving utility. The privacy and utility gradients are near-orthogonal ([MATH]93.8[MATH]), so reducing privacy leakage leaves utility almost unchanged. On four public PhysioNet databases, REAN achieves the strongest privacy--utility balance among raw ECG signal baselines. It drives re-identification to chance (0.96[MATH]0.00), keeps arrhythmia macro-AUROC at the clean level (Clean 0.9982 vs.\ REAN 0.9991), and maintains re-identification protection under unseen privacy-classifier architectures.
tldr: This paper proposes a reconstruction-aware ECG anonymization method to balance privacy and utility.
motivation: ECG signals can be used as biometric identifiers, leading to privacy risks when shared. Existing anonymizers suffer from a privacy-utility trade-off.
method: REAN uses a 1-D U-Net trained with losses from frozen privacy and utility classifiers, leveraging near-orthogonal gradients to reduce privacy leakage while preserving utility.
result: On four public databases, REAN reduces re-identification to chance level while maintaining arrhythmia classification performance (macro-AUROC 0.9991 vs clean 0.9982).
conclusion: REAN achieves a strong privacy-utility balance for ECG anonymization, demonstrating the effectiveness of orthogonal gradient updates.

title: Poster: Mind The Gap -- Characterizing The Temporal Blind Spot Between Gsb And Dns Resolution
authors: Tomer Gal, Fujiao Ji, Doowon Kim, Harel Israel Berger
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Google Safe Browsing (GSB) and DNS resolution operate concurrently during browser navigation, yet their packet-level synchronization remains understudied. This work characterizes the timing gap (\(\Delta_{time}\)) between GSB-related query close events and parallel DNS resolution responses, identifying a consistent temporal offset with potential security relevance. Using packet-capture analysis across general and CNAME-domain datasets, we observe positive timing gaps in approximately 79\% of measurements. In these instances, DNS responses lag behind GSB-related query closures with median delays of 67-79 ms and maximum delays surpassing 2,400 ms. These empirical results highlight a measurable window within the browsing workflow. We suggest that such temporal inconsistencies, particularly in complex CNAME-domain resolutions, may create a security-relevant timing precondition under DNS-manipulation threat models. These results provide a foundation for further research into timing-based risks and mitigations in browser safety mechanisms.
tldr: This paper characterizes the timing gap between Google Safe Browsing queries and DNS resolution, identifying a potential security vulnerability.
motivation: The synchronization between GSB and DNS resolution during browser navigation is understudied, and timing gaps may create security risks.
method: Packet-capture analysis across general and CNAME-domain datasets to measure the temporal offset between GSB query closures and DNS responses.
result: Positive timing gaps in ~79% of measurements, with median delays of 67-79 ms and maximum delays over 2,400 ms.
conclusion: The observed temporal inconsistencies, especially in CNAME-domain resolutions, may create a security-relevant timing precondition under DNS-manipulation threat models.

title: The Masks We (Think We) Wear: Privacy Threats Of Browser-Extension Wallets In The Web3 Ecosystem
authors: Weihong Wang, Yana Dimova, Victor Vansteenkiste, Tom van Goethem, Tom van Cutsem
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptocurrency wallets are the primary interface for managing pseudonymous blockchain addresses, viewing balances, and interacting with Web3 applications. Although users typically assume that their addresses remain independent of each other unless intentionally revealed, modern wallets routinely communicate with both blockchain infrastructure and decentralized applications (dApps), generating network-side and web-side signals that may undermine this assumption. In this paper, we identify and formalize five privacy threats that arise directly from wallets interacting with the network and the web browser. Using large-scale dynamic measurements of 85 of the most popular Chrome Web Store browser-extension wallets (representing 35.16 million users), we observe that routine remote procedure call (RPC) operations leak structural links between a user's addresses; that the majority of Ethereum wallets implement permission revocation inconsistently and continue to expose previously revoked addresses across sessions; and that many wallets inject their provider interfaces into cross-origin iframes, enabling passive cross-site tracking beyond dApps and potentially real-world identity deanonymization without user interaction. Taken together, our results show that these wallet behaviors leak sensitive information that can be used to link multiple addresses to the same user, track wallet users across sessions and sites, and connect their browsing activity to their on-chain wealth. We discuss practical mitigations and show that many of these threats can be substantially reduced through improved wallet implementation, stronger privacy considerations in ecosystem standards, and stricter controls over provider exposure. Our results highlight the need for standardized, privacy-preserving wallet architectures.
tldr: This paper studies privacy threats in browser-extension cryptocurrency wallets, focusing on address linkage and cross-site tracking.
motivation: Users assume blockchain addresses are pseudonymous and independent, but wallet behaviors may leak information that undermines this assumption.
method: Large-scale dynamic measurements of 85 Chrome Web Store browser-extension wallets, analyzing RPC operations, permission revocation, and provider injection.
result: Routine RPC operations leak structural links between addresses; most wallets handle permission revocation inconsistently; many inject providers into cross-origin iframes enabling cross-site tracking.
conclusion: Wallet implementations and ecosystem standards need improvement to mitigate these privacy threats.

title: Claimed Or Attested? A Commit-Signature Dataset And Identity Trust Tiers Across The World Of Code
authors: Audris Mockus
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An author string in a git commit is free text the committer typed, so identity resolution over a global commit corpus rests on a claim that nothing in the commit verifies. A cryptographically signed commit is different: it binds the commit to a key the committer controls, and when that key ties back to a real-world identity the git identity becomes attested rather than merely claimed. We release the first commit-signature axis for the World of Code (WoC), extracted for the V2604 collection.
